articles_hidden.title: A herbivore-induced plant volatile facilitates group foraging in locusts
articles_hidden.authors: Lingzhi Shi, Jinmeng Guo, Jinxi Yuan, Yan Yan, Jiancai Li, Guirong Wang, Bill S. Hansson, Hetan Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Plants have evolved sophisticated defense strategies against herbivory, often releasing volatile compounds upon attack to deter further feeding. Here, we demonstrate the induced volatile S-linalool promotes phase- and stage-specific group foraging in the migratory locust ( Locusta migratoria ). We show that S-linalool, a volatile whose emission increases more than 10-fold following damage by gregarious nymphs, acts as a potent attractant that drives other nymphs to aggregate and feed on previously attacked rice plants. Mechanistically, we identified the olfactory receptor LmOR49 that detects S-linalool and used genome editing to make this receptor nonfunctional, thereby abolishing both electrophysiological responses and behavioral attraction. We also inactivated rice genes required for S-linalool biosynthesis, abolishing its emission, rendering plants unattractive, and disrupting locust feeding preference. Although feeding on previously attacked plants provides no detectable direct fitness benefit under our experimental conditions, prior locust feeding suppresses the accumulation of deterrent metabolites, potentially increasing plant palatability for subsequent feeding. S-linalool thus serves as an olfactory cue that guides gregarious nymphs toward previously attacked, more palatable plants. Collectively, these findings uncover a comprehensive mechanism whereby a plant defense volatile is exploited by an insect herbivore to promote group foraging, broadening our understanding of plant–insect interactions and suggesting molecular targets for locust control.

articles_hidden.title: Quantifying (de)mixing of disordered proteins in molecular dynamics simulations
articles_hidden.authors: William Morton, Robert Vácha
articles_hidden.abstract: Biomolecular condensates control the spatial and temporal organization of cellular biochemistry. Their architectures often arise from complex, multicomponent mixtures governed by weak, multivalent interactions between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins. However, current approaches lack generalizable metrics to determine whether IDRs will mix or segregate within condensates. Here, we present a domain decomposition method (DDM) that accurately determines phase concentrations without identifying condensate interfaces. When tested against 399 IDR simulations, the DDM recovers dense- and dilute-phase concentrations within 1% agreement of established surface-based methods. By calculating spatial variances to map three-dimensional organization, this approach successfully distinguishes homogeneous mixing from surface enrichment, core–shell architectures, and complete segregation. Applying this continuous metric to 2,068 binary mixtures of 32 distinct IDRs, we demonstrate that physicochemical similarity strongly promotes mixing. Hydrophobic IDRs mixed promiscuously across all partner chemistries, whereas charged sequences mixed in a way highly sensitive to charge complementarity, forming the most stable condensates as net charge approached zero. Compared with experimental networks, our IDR-only simulations predicted the partitioning preferences for 10 of 13 proteins, with discrepancies accurately isolating cases where colocalization strictly requires RNA or folded domains. Quantifying mixing in this way provides a robust and reproducible method for predicting IDR interactomes and understanding the composition of complex cellular condensates.

articles_hidden.title: Neuronal IL-34 programs microglial activity via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis to constrain neuroinflammation following brain ischemia
articles_hidden.authors: Minshu Li, Xu Zhou, Ran Li, Hanchen Liu, Caiyun Qi, Wenjun Zhang, Yali Han, Tingyu Yin, Sarah Wu, Yan Pan, Decai Tian, Tao Yan, Jie Zhou, Xiaochun Chen, Qiang Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Brain ischemia induces robust neuroinflammation driven by microglial activation, yet whether ischemic neurons actively reprogram microglial phenotypes to limit inflammation remains elusive. Here, we identify neuronal interleukin-34 (IL-34) as a critical immunomodulatory signal that maintains microglial homeostasis after cerebral ischemia. We demonstrate that ischemic injury augments IL-34-CSF1R signaling between neurons and microglia. Neuron-specific overexpression of Il34 (Syn1- Il34 tg mice) attenuated infarct volume and neurodeficits after middle cerebral artery occlusion, whereas neuronal Il34 knockdown exacerbated brain injury. Microglial depletion abolished IL-34-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting microglia as essential effectors. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that neuronal IL-34 preserved homeostatic microglial signatures ( P2ry12, Cx3cr1, Tgfbr1 ), while suppressing inflammatory activities ( Il1b, Tnf, Cxcl2 ) through upregulation of the transcription factor MEF2C. Mechanistically, IL-34 activated TGF-β signaling in microglia and inhibition of TGF-β signaling abolished the protective effects of IL-34, whereas microglia-specific Mef2c overexpression rescued neuroprotection despite TGF-β blockade. Thus, ischemic neurons deploy IL-34 to orchestrate the immunoregulatory activity of microglia via the TGF-β–MEF2C axis, representing a previously unrecognized endogenous mechanism counteracting neuroinflammation. Our study reveals neuronal IL-34 as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

articles_hidden.title: Inactivation of the RB1 and PTPN14 tumor suppressors cooperatively enables the lifespan extension activity of the human papillomavirus E7 oncoprotein
articles_hidden.authors: Pushkal Sinduvadi Ramesh, Angelo A. Nicolaci, Leah E. Graham, Joangela Nouel, Kevin Xu, Jennifer M. Binning, Karl Munger, Elizabeth A. White
articles_hidden.abstract: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) E7 proteins bind and inactivate host cellular tumor suppressors and are essential for the immortalization of primary human keratinocytes. E7 proteins from high- and low-risk HPV genotypes bind directly to at least two tumor suppressors, RB1 and PTPN14, and inactivate both. We previously characterized mutations in high-risk HPV E7 proteins that selectively abrogate the ability of E7 to bind either RB1 or PTPN14. Here, we established a genetic complementation system using the E7 mutants defective for binding to RB1 or PTPN14. Neither mutant alone could extend the lifespan of primary keratinocytes. When expressed together, the mutants could, like wild-type high-risk HPV E7, extend keratinocyte lifespan. Both high- and low-risk E7 reduced PTPN14 protein levels and reduced expression of keratinocyte differentiation genes, whereas only high-risk E7 reduced steady-state RB1 levels and induced E2F-dependent genes. Depletion of either RB1 or PTPN14 could cooperate with low-risk HPV6 E7 to extend keratinocyte lifespan. Our findings advance the model that inactivation of at least two tumor suppressors is required for the lifespan extension activity of high-risk HPV E7.

articles_hidden.title: Preemptive solving of future problems: Multitask Preplay in humans and machines
articles_hidden.authors: Wilka Carvalho, Sam Hall-McMaster, Honglak Lee, Samuel J. Gershman
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans can pursue a near-infinite variety of tasks, but typically can only pursue a small number at the same time. We hypothesize that humans leverage experience on one task to preemptively learn solutions to other tasks that were accessible but not pursued. We formalize this idea as “Multitask Preplay”, an algorithm that replays experience on one task as the starting point for “preplay”—counterfactual simulation of an accessible but unpursued task. Preplay is used to learn a predictive representation that can support fast, adaptive task performance later on. When implemented within deep reinforcement learning, it predicts human generalization to novel tasks more accurately than traditional planning and predictive representation methods across grid-worlds and a 2D Minecraft domain. Additionally, Multitask Preplay improves an artificial agent’s ability to generalize to new environments sharing task co-occurrence structure. These findings demonstrate that Multitask Preplay is a scalable theory of human counterfactual learning and generalization; endowing artificial agents with this capacity can significantly improve their performance in challenging multitask environments.

articles_hidden.title: Paul R. Ehrlich: Visionary pioneer and public scientist for nature and humanity
articles_hidden.authors: Gretchen C. Daily, Rodolfo Dirzo, Carl Folke, John P. Holdren, Simon A. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract: Paul R. Ehrlich is legendary for his scientific insight and impact—and even more so for bringing science to the public through writing, speaking, and, most famously, twenty-some appearances on the Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson. He was quick-witted—he would readily add quick-tempered, with chagrin—and could bring down a house. Paul cherished deep friendships and nature. He loved collaborating with his wife of 71 years, Anne H. Ehrlich, and with innumerable students and colleagues all over the world. He made transformative contributions of astonishing range, including in ecology and evolution, biodiversity and conservation, human population and overconsumption, and the integration of ecology and economics. He was deeply committed to racial and social justice, reflected in his actions and writing.

articles_hidden.title: A periplasmic regulator establishes adaptive impermeability to control carbapenem entry
articles_hidden.authors: Verena Ducret, Catarina Gonçalves Milho, Diego Gonzalez, Karl Perron
articles_hidden.abstract: Outer-membrane permeability is a major determinant of antibiotic susceptibility in Gram-negative bacteria and is generally thought to be controlled through transcriptional regulation of porin expression. Here we identify the small periplasmic protein PtrA as a regulator of OprD-dependent carbapenem permeability in Pseudomonas aeruginosa . PtrA promotes imipenem resistance without altering OprD abundance, associates with OprD-containing membrane complexes and reduces intracellular imipenem entry. Using zinc and copper as complementary physiological signals, we show that PtrA-mediated permeability control is mechanistically distinct from CzcRS-dependent repression of oprD and precedes transcriptional porin depletion. These findings define a two-phase mechanism in which rapid periplasmic regulation provides an immediate adaptive response before transcriptional remodeling of the outer membrane. Our work identifies adaptive impermeability as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking environmental sensing to dynamic control of bacterial outer-membrane permeability.

articles_hidden.title: Anterior cingulate cortex neurons parse speakers in a natural cocktail party
articles_hidden.authors: Arthur Lefevre, Vikram Pal Singh, Timothy J. Tyree, Jingwen Li, Pia Giraudet, Jean-René Duhamel, Cory T. Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: The cocktail party problem—parsing relevant voices from competing speakers—has traditionally been studied as a sensory challenge for auditory cortex. Yet in natural communication, identifying speakers and coordinating interaction are inherently social processes. Here we recorded single neurons from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC, area 24) in freely moving marmosets engaged in spontaneous vocal exchanges within a noisy colony environment. ACC neurons selectively encoded vocalizations from a social partner versus other callers in the scene, effectively parsing speakers in the acoustic mixture. This selectivity was preserved even when vocalizations overlapped in time, indicating robustness to background interference. Apart from perception, ACC population activity represented vocal production, call type, and whether calls occurred within vocal turn-taking exchanges. Behaviorally, marmosets adjusted vocal timing based on the surrounding acoustic scene, and these interaction contexts were reliably reflected in ACC activity. Together, these findings suggest that neurons in ACC play a role in parsing conspecific speakers during communication in a natural “cocktail party,” linking auditory scene analysis with social monitoring and coordinated interactions.

articles_hidden.title: Influence of noninertial dynamics on static quantum resource theories
articles_hidden.authors: Saveetha Harikrishnan, Tim Byrnes, Chandrashekar Radhakrishnan
articles_hidden.abstract: The effect of noninertial dynamics on static quantum resource theories is investigated. To this end, we first show the equivalence between noninertial effects and a completely positive, trace-preserving (CPTP) map. In this formulation, the Unruh effect is equivalent to a bosonic amplifier channel. The effect of this map on a generic quantum resource is investigated by studying the role of the CPTP map on the three core ingredients of a resource theory, namely, the free states, the free operations, and the resource quantifiers. We show several general statements can be made about these three components of a resource theory in the presence of noninertial motion.

articles_hidden.title: An ensemble of functionally distinct factors enables spatial quality control during proteasome base assembly
articles_hidden.authors: Eshita Das, Linh Le, Richard Kim, James D. Orth, Soyeon Park
articles_hidden.abstract: The proteasome is an essential mediator of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and a complex molecular machine. Hallmarks of de novo proteasome assembly include dedicated chaperones and many subunits, culminating into major assembly intermediates such as the base. Emerging evidence suggests that proteasome assembly is subject to extensive quality control (QC). To understand mechanisms of QC, we examined a crucial assembly checkpoint during base assembly. Our findings reveal sequential mechanisms of QC, in which a checkpoint complex is first assembled, then sequestered into the nucleus, away from ongoing proteasome assembly in the cytoplasm. Assembly of this checkpoint complex depends on noncanonical ubiquitination of the Nas2 chaperone. The Nas2 ubiquitin chain functions as a scaffold by binding the Rpn13 ubiquitin receptor, which is distantly positioned within the same complex. Rpn13 also positions the ubiquitin chain to its neighboring Hul5 ubiquitin ligase, for continual chain elongation to further stabilize this complex. Ubiquitin-mediated assembly enables spatial sequestration of this checkpoint complex through its intrinsic nuclear localization signal (NLS). This NLS on Rpt4 specifically targets this checkpoint complex into the nucleus, emphasizing the importance of spatial compartmentalization. Our findings reveal that proteasome assembly integrates multiple functionally distinct components as QC factors (1 assembly chaperone, 2 ubiquitin regulators, and 1 NLS) to distinguish correct vs. incorrect assembly events en route to a proteasome holoenzyme. These components are not simply passengers in assembly intermediates with their activities reserved for mature proteasomes, but their fundamental functions in cellular proteolysis may begin by first ensuring the accuracy of proteasome assembly.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking broad diet breadth as a sign of scarcity: A 50,000-y record of subsistence from northwestern Australia
articles_hidden.authors: Tiina Manne, Erin Mein, Jane Balme, Sue O’Connor, Ken Aplin, Peter Veth
articles_hidden.abstract: The prey choice model, widely applied in archaeological reconstructions of Pleistocene diet, predicts that people will initially focus on a narrow suite of high-ranked prey before broadening their diet to include lower-ranked species as necessitated by subsistence needs. However, evidence from arid and semiarid northern Australia challenges this assumption. Archaeological faunal records demonstrate that a broad diet was established early and persisted through the Holocene. We argue that these diverse diets do not indicate resource scarcity, but rather represent an ideal strategy for exploiting abundant, low-risk hidden, or cryptic prey, as well as high-risk, conspicuous prey within an environment characterized by unpredictable rainfall. This pattern also necessitates reconceptualizing traditional notions of prey rank and dietary breadth. Rather than adhering to static prey rankings, northern Australian peoples skillfully adapted their hunting strategies in response to fluctuating nutritional content and pursuit costs of different species. The most successful subsistence strategy in this region was therefore one of high responsiveness and flexibility, manifesting as a consistently broad diet. This case study suggests that the relationship between human dietary breadth and resource abundance is more nuanced in situations of abundant, cryptic prey.

articles_hidden.title: Gap test–inspired crack-parallel tension tests of fracture of soft-knitted polymer composites simulated by microplane triads
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoxiao Ding, Yanzhao Niu, Yang Zhao, Hongshun Chen, Chanhyeong Bae, Anh Tay Nguyen, Horacio D. Espinosa, Zdeněk P. Bažant, Jian Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Soft composites are increasingly used in wearable and soft robotic systems, as advances in material architecture enable greater damage tolerance under large deformation. In these mesoscale architectures, the crack-parallel stresses modify the crack initiation and growth in the opening-mode fracture. Emulating the gap test, we introduce a fracture test to quantify how the superposed crack-parallel tension affects the maximum load (i.e., the load capacity) and the load-deflection curve. A Mode I (opening mode) center-notched tensioned strip is used because its advantages in generating crack-parallel tension outweigh its hypothetical disadvantages with possible instability of crack jumps at two competing crack fronts. We develop and experimentally validate a continuum model that captures the nonlinear behavior and progressive damage of knitted composites. To this end, we introduce an ensemble of oriented microplane triads tangential to the yarn at characteristic points of the yarn loop within a repetitive unit cell of the knit. The triads ensure the yarn-polymer transfer of all normal and shear stress components at each characteristic point. The experimentally calibrated computational model provides a tool to predict the effect of crack-parallel tension on the changes of load capacity and of the effective fracture energy of knitted polymer composites, enabling rational design of these composites in engineering applications such as wearables and soft robotics.

articles_hidden.title: Conditions for runaway ruptures during reservoir operations: Magnitude–frequency distribution implications and application to Groningen
articles_hidden.authors: Qian Shi, Alexis Sáez, Linxuan Li, Kyungjae Im, Stephen Bourne, Jan van Elk, Jean-Philippe Avouac
articles_hidden.abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of an induced seismic rupture propagating from a gas reservoir into the underburden. We use linear elastic fracture mechanics to determine the conditions for self-arrested or runaway ruptures. We derive a phase diagram in which the model parameters (the reservoir thickness, the reservoir pressure depletion, background stress, and fracture energy) are combined into two dimensionless parameters. We apply the analysis to the seismicity induced by gas extraction from the Groningen gas field, where earthquakes have remained confined to the close vicinity of the reservoir. We invert the observations for the model parameters. They indicate subcritical initial stress on the underburden faults, meaning that runaway ruptures are possible in principle, but the conditions required for such events to have happened were most likely not met in reality. The model reproduces the spatial and temporal patterns of observed maximum earthquake magnitudes, and the significant deficit of M > 3.0 events compared to the expectation from the Gutenberg–Richter relationship. This tapering implies that the expected maximum magnitude is nearly insensitive to the total number of induced earthquakes and strongly controlled by the reservoir thickness and pressure depletion. Because the forecast is probabilistic and accounts for uncertainties in the model parameters, it does not exclude runaway ruptures; but such events are found to be unlikely. The model offers an operational framework to forecast earthquake magnitudes by constraining the physical model with measurable parameters.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis of plastid Mg 2+ transport by the magnesium channel MGT10 in Arabidopsis
articles_hidden.authors: Chao Wang, Aiyan Huang, Lingjie Lin, Jinda Ou, Qiqi Zhang, Yingying Li, Chengcheng Liang, Xiumei Xu, Wei Wang, Minrui Fan, Lixin Zhang, Peiqiang Feng
articles_hidden.abstract: Magnesium ions (Mg 2+ ) are vital for photosynthesis, serving as central metal ions in chlorophyll molecules and activating RuBisCO. MGT10 is the only member of the CorA/MRS2 superfamily bound to the chloroplast envelope membrane, where it mediates Mg 2+ uptake and homeostasis in chloroplasts. Despite its importance, the mechanism of MGT10-mediated Mg 2+ transport remains unclear. Here, we report cryoelectron microscopy structures of Arabidopsis MGT10 in two conformations, along with functional characterizations. MGT10 assembles into a homopentameric structure with a central tunnel connecting the transmembrane and soluble domains. A constriction ring consisting of five conserved arginine residues arranged asymmetrically in the tunnel is crucial for Mg 2+ conduction. Our structures reveal an unexpected gating mechanism involving a conformational transition from a symmetric closed state to an asymmetric, putatively open state. In addition, we identified an intramolecular disulfide bond within each soluble domain as a unique structural feature of MGT10. Structural and functional analyses show that this disulfide bond is required for MGT10’s structural integrity and for regulating its function in photosynthesis. Taken together, our findings provide insights into Mg 2+ transport and regulatory mechanisms of MGT10 in chloroplasts.

articles_hidden.title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality
articles_hidden.authors: Claudia Lainscsek, Pariya Salami, Simon Dräger, Adi R. Bulsara, Sydney S. Cash, Terrence J. Sejnowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that “Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)” further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Four phases and temporal threshold of population calcium response during locomotion in cortical astrocytes
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Fedotova, Alexey Brazhe, Alexey Semyanov
articles_hidden.abstract: Calcium activity is a major form of astrocyte excitability. Astrocytic calcium events arise spontaneously and in response to behavior, but how unitary events shape population-level activity remains unclear. Using two-photon imaging in the primary somatosensory cortex of awake mice running on a freely rotating disk, we analyzed calcium dynamics during quiescence and locomotion. During quiescence, population fluctuations were driven mainly by the co-occurrence of new events rather than by their enlargement. During locomotion, responses progressed through four phases: emergence of new events, their merging into a superevent, fragmentation, and an afterburst. These responses combined the progressive recruitment of active regions with amplification of a reproducible spatial calcium pattern. New events emerged within the first seconds after locomotion onset, indicating a rapid astrocytic response. A full population response required about 5 s of locomotion: Shorter episodes failed to develop the superevent and produced markedly smaller responses. In suprathreshold episodes, the superevent displayed a reproducible ΔF/F pattern. Hotspots within this pattern had shorter latencies and were also more active during quiescence. A dynamic mode decomposition with control model driven by synthetic or real locomotion inputs reproduced the response phases, temporal threshold, and superevent pattern. These findings show that locomotion-evoked astrocytic calcium activity is an ordered, threshold-dependent population process with reproducible spatiotemporal structure that can be approximated by a low-dimensional dynamical system.

articles_hidden.title: Physicochemical microenvironments within biomolecular condensates govern reaction kinetics beyond mass-action effects
articles_hidden.authors: Jangwon Bae, Kibeom Hong, Donghyuk Lee, Jaebum Jun, Yongwon Jung
articles_hidden.abstract: Cells utilize phase separation to compartmentalize biochemical reactions within biomolecular condensates. Although these compartments can enhance reaction rates by concentrating reactants, how they modulate kinetics beyond mass-action effects remains poorly understood. Here, using spontaneous protein ligation as a model reaction, we examined how the physicochemical microenvironment within condensates modulates reaction kinetics. We systematically analyzed condensates formed by folded PRM–SH3 scaffolds and intrinsically disordered proteins (LAF, TAF, and FUS). We designed a proximity-sensitive client probe to assess excluded-volume-driven increases in effective reactant concentration. In parallel, we characterized condensate hydrophilicity and associated changes in water activity, identifying these properties as additional key kinetic determinants. Together, our findings elucidate how effective concentration and hydrophilicity jointly regulate biochemical reactions within condensates.

articles_hidden.title: ACSS2 modulates endothelial glycolysis in angiogenesis
articles_hidden.authors: Yunyun Wang, Qingqiao Zha, Rong-Mo Zhang, Hong Chen, He Cai, Jingyi Xiang, Yaohui Kou, Cong Qiu, Lei Zhang, Michael Simons, Luyang Yu, Xiaolong Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract: Endothelial cells (ECs) sustain high glycolytic flux and display remarkable metabolic plasticity. Although molecular pathways regulating endothelial glycolysis are well characterized, metabolic mechanisms underlying hypoxia-induced glycolytic activation during angiogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we show that acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (ACSS2) serves as a critical metabolic modulator, coupling acetate utilization with glycolytic flux to control EC function and angiogenesis. The high level of ACSS2-mediated acetate-to-acetyl-CoA conversion in angiogenic front ECs sustains acetyl-CoA levels, which are essential for EC proliferation and retinal vascularization. Conversely, endothelial-specific Acss2 deletion disrupts pathological angiogenesis and normalizes tumor vasculature. Mechanistically, ACSS2 maintains hypoxia-inducible factor 1α transcriptional activity and stabilizes glucose transporter 1, thereby preserving glycolysis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 knockdown rescues metabolic and functional defects in ACSS2-deficient ECs, revealing the vital role of acetyl-CoA homeostasis in modulating hypoxic endothelial metabolism. Taken together, these data establish ACSS2 as a pivotal regulator of vascular development and suggest that targeting acetate metabolism may be an effective way to modulate pathological angiogenesis.

articles_hidden.title: A chromatin biology assessment of AlphaFold3
articles_hidden.authors: Yash Bhargava, Sanim Rahman, Cynthia Wolberger
articles_hidden.abstract: Biomolecular structure prediction tools such as AlphaFold have achieved remarkable success in predicting structures of single proteins and multiprotein complexes. AlphaFold3 now incorporates the capability to model complexes containing nucleic acids and chemically modified side chains. Investigators can now predict structures of proteins bound to chromatin, where interactions with nucleosomal DNA and histone posttranslational modifications (PTMs) converge to control genome function. To evaluate its robustness in modeling chromatin complexes, we benchmarked AlphaFold3 on 115 structures containing nucleosomes whose coordinates were released by the Protein Data Bank after the training set cutoff date. We find that AlphaFold3 excels at predicting interactions with the histone octamer core and with PTMs. By contrast, AlphaFold3 struggles to predict structures of chromatin factors that primarily engage nucleosomal DNA, notably transcription factors and chromatin remodelers. We also show that AlphaFold3 can faithfully recapitulate known PTM recognition patterns, matching experimentally determined specificity profiles. This assessment of the capabilities and limitations of AlphaFold3 in chromatin structural biology provides a roadmap for its effective application to studies of chromatin regulation and PTM readout, while identifying key areas for future refinement of algorithms for predicting interactions between proteins and nucleic acids.

articles_hidden.title: Cryo-EM provides insight into how the Staphylococcus aureus IsdH receptor removes hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin complex
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Soule, Brendan J. Mahoney, Andrew K. Goring, Joseph A. Loo, Jose A. Rodriguez, Robert T. Clubb
articles_hidden.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus extracts hemin from human hemoglobin (Hb) to overcome host-imposed iron limitation. How it recovers Hb-bound hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin (Hb:Hp) complex, the major circulating form of Hb outside red blood cells, remains unclear. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy, biophysical measurements, and solution kinetics to define how the S. aureus IsdH surface receptor extracts hemin from Hb:Hp. A 3.1 Å cryo-EM structure of Hb:Hp bound by full-length IsdH reveals that its N-terminal NEAT domain (N1) anchors it to αHb, whereas its downstream N2N3 extraction unit engages βHb to remove its hemin. The receptor engages Hb:Hp differently than isolated Hb, because N-linked glycans on haptoglobin bias the extraction unit toward βHb, sterically occluding its access to αHb while still permitting engagement by N1. Kinetic assays show that IsdH actively accelerates hemin release from Hb:Hp. Three-dimensional variability analysis indicates that this likely occurs via a dynamic interface in which receptor motions reposition the extraction unit relative to βHb, collectively supporting a model in which IsdH transiently perturbs the F-helix to promote hemin extraction. Alignment of that model with a previously determined CD163:Hb:Hp structure shows how IsdH may disrupt Hb:Hp recognition by macrophage and monocyte CD163 receptors, helping to explain how it may hinder clearance of Hb:Hp from circulation. In aggregate, these results help define the structural basis for hemin extraction from Hb:Hp and how IsdH may subvert receptor-mediated clearance of the Hb:Hp complex.

articles_hidden.title: Preassembled NLR complexes shape immune sensitivity and defense
articles_hidden.authors: Jianbin Su, Walter Gassmann

articles_hidden.title: Senescence markers diverge in space, timing, and phenotypic relevance during skin aging in mice
articles_hidden.authors: Burcin Duan Sahbaz, Hazal Ozturk Gurgen, Brandon Lamotte, Shiva Puttagunta, Ethan Durham, Amanda Garrido, Burcu Can, Maria E. Fernandez, Ericka Oglesby, Christopher H. Morrell, Elin Lehrmann, Alexandra N. Rindone, Christopher Cherry, Prarthana S. Daswani, Simonetta Camandola, Michel Bernier, Benjamin D. Cosgrove, Supriyo De, Darren J. Baker, Jennifer Elisseeff, Nathan L. Price, Rafael de Cabo
articles_hidden.abstract: The cell theory of aging posits that senescent cells accumulate with age, altering their environment and causing functional organ decline. The dynamics of their accumulation during normal aging and the extent to which it contributes to age-associated damage and disease remain unclear. Using the Study of Longitudinal Aging in Mice, which tracks two strains in both sexes, we identified skin health as a strong predictor of frailty. Quantification of three canonical senescence-associated markers (p16, p21, and γH2AX) in the skin of 320 animals showed variable effects of age on marker abundance: p16 increased with age, whereas p21 and γH2AX showed little or nonuniform changes. Associations between marker burden and age-related phenotypes were highly heterogeneous and varied by marker, sex, and strain. These findings underscore a complex, context-dependent relationship between senescence-associated markers and aging phenotypes, challenging the view that senescent cell accumulation uniformly drives organ decline.

articles_hidden.title: Protein spherical nucleic acids enable multivalent display of TLR9 agonists for enhanced cancer immunotherapy
articles_hidden.authors: Taokun Luo, Zhenyu Han, Young Jun Kim, Vinzenz Mayer, Alex Cushing, Chad A. Mirkin
articles_hidden.abstract: Precise control over nanoparticle composition and molecular architecture remains a fundamental challenge in nanomedicine, limiting systematic exploration of therapeutic design and biological function. Here, we report structurally defined protein spherical nucleic acids (ProSNAs) comprising ferritin nanocages densely functionalized with Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) agonist, immunostimulatory oligonucleotide shell for cancer immunotherapy. ProSNAs are rapidly internalized by immune cells, elicit potent innate immune activation, and exhibit prolonged intratumoral retention with preferential uptake by myeloid cells. These responses promote dendritic cell maturation, polarize macrophages toward an antitumor phenotype, and stimulate robust CD8 + T cell–mediated immunity. Across murine melanoma, colon adenocarcinoma, and triple-negative breast cancer models, a single intratumoral administration of ProSNAs induces durable tumor regression, suppresses metastatic progression, and synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade. Taken together, these findings establish ProSNAs as a structurally defined, myeloid-targeting nanomedicine platform for programmable cancer immunotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: Human retinal capillary network analysis using vascular interconnectivity optical coherence tomography angiography
articles_hidden.authors: Yunchan Hwang, Jungeun Won, Muhammad Usman Jamil, Benjamin Potsaid, Nadia K. Waheed, James G. Fujimoto
articles_hidden.abstract: The human retina is perfused by capillary plexuses at distinct inner-retinal depths. Interconnections among these plexuses are critical for perfusion, but are difficult to quantify using 2D en face optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA). Diabetic retinopathy (DR) involves extensive microvascular remodeling, however the topological changes, especially at the interplexus level, are challenging to assess in vivo. We introduce Network Analysis using Vascular Interconnectivity (NAVI) OCTA, a framework that reconstructs the 3D retinal capillary network across the superficial vascular (SVP), intermediate capillary (ICP), and deep capillary (DCP) plexuses. The reconstructed macula-wide vasculature contains more than 10,000 vessel segments, and can be quantitatively analyzed using network representation. This method reveals a divergent alteration in interplexus connectivity in early DR: superficial-to-intermediate connections decrease, while intermediate-to-deep connections increase. This finding is consistent with previous histological studies, but is quantitatively measured in vivo in the human retina, opening the possibility for longitudinal studies of capillary remodeling. In addition to size-based metrics (e.g., vessel length or area), NAVI can quantify recurrent small-scale connectivity patterns (motifs). Finally, joint connectivity-hemodynamics analysis is demonstrated in eyes with DR, where capillary topology and flow speed can be quantified using a single OCTA acquisition. NAVI OCTA is a scalable, computational framework that supports analysis of retinal vasculature as a network and provides an in vivo approach to study capillary remodeling in early DR.

articles_hidden.title: Lactate-rich tumor employs the KAT5–HIF1α axis to modulate the activity of the hypoxia pathway and facilitates tumor progression
articles_hidden.authors: Zhaoxiang Wang, Zhengyan Liang, Yingzhi Chen, Xia Kong, Zhiguo Wang, Panpan Zhu, Hewen Ye, Jiao Yuan, Jiayue Wen, Weixian Zhou, Ying Xue, Yongkang Zou, Zhiwei He, Junzhi Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Substantial evidence shows that hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) up-regulates glycolytic enzymes and promotes lactate production, which contributes to “Warburg Effect.” Nevertheless, the impact of lactate or lactylation modification on hypoxia signaling pathways within the tumor microenvironment remains largely unclear. Here, we report that lactate can induce the upregulation of hypoxia pathway activity in a HIF1α-dependent manner. We identified that KAT5 as a lysine lactyltransferase of HIF1α and the “writer” responsible for lactylation at HIF1α K389, K460, K674, and K682, and HDAC2 as a HIF1α de-lactylase. The lactylation-deficient mutant of HIF1α (HIF1α 4KR ) reduced HIF1α stability, along with down-regulating hypoxia-mediated angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis, and glycolysis. Mechanistically, the HIF1α 4KR mutant enhances the binding of HIF1α to von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein (VHL), facilitating its degradation. MG149, a KAT5 inhibitor, can enhance the efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)-based combination immunotherapy in a murine model by suppressing hypoxia pathway activity in tumor cells and potentiating the cytotoxic function of CD8 + T cells. Clinically, lactylated HIF1α and KAT5 are up-regulated in breast cancer tissues compared with adjacent tissues. Notably, elevated levels of HIF1α lactylation and KAT5 expression were observed in resistant cancer specimens from triple-negative breast cancer patients who had undergone neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Our results indicate that the tumor lactate microenvironment promotes the formation of the tumor hypoxic microenvironment by hijacking and lactylating HIF1α, and the KAT5–HIF1α Kla axis presents a promising therapeutic target for hypoxic tumors.

articles_hidden.title: Coevolving gene networks underlying a phenotypic syndrome revealed via integrating comparative genomic and microevolutionary analyses
articles_hidden.authors: Saurav Baral, Sridhar Halali, Mats Ittonen, Klaus Fischer, Karl Gotthard, Christopher W. Wheat
articles_hidden.abstract: Complex adaptive traits often comprise interacting, coevolving phenotypes that together for a syndrome that is shaped by multiple genetic loci. While using intraspecific variation is an established approach for investigating syndromes, such polymorphism typically captures only a subset of syndrome traits. Diapause, an alternative developmental pathway that evolved independently in many species to synchronize life cycles with resource availability, exemplifies this challenge. While subsets of this essential phenotype have long been studied at a single species level, the genomic basis of the full diapause syndrome remains poorly understood. This paucity of insights has fueled a long-standing debate about how life cycle synchronization evolves and whether convergent phenotypes employ shared mechanisms. Using a comparative genomic analysis spanning diverse diapause transitions in butterflies, we identified a large network of coevolving genes unique to diapausing species. The network is composed of functional modules spanning circadian regulation, metabolism, and cell cycle control. We tested whether this macroevolutionary scale network predicts microevolutionary dynamics, hypothesizing that this network is the polygenic architecture underlying the diapause syndrome. Analyses revealed that allelic variation in the diapause network is significantly enriched in signatures of local adaptation across latitudes, but only in diapausing species. Thus, we empirically show that diapause evolves through modular, coevolving gene networks, components of which impact intraspecific variation in diapause. Using this integrative perspective on a complex phenotype opens a horizon of inquiry for understanding seasonal adaptation across evolutionary scales, while demonstrating the power of integrating comparative genomics with microevolutionary dynamics to dissect complex phenotypic syndromes.

articles_hidden.title: Ctf4 chaperones parental histones to preserve epigenetic memory
articles_hidden.authors: Yuan Gao, Xiangyi Yan, Wai Hei Lam, Chaoqi Yang, Zhan Yin, Yan Chit Hui, Yan Chen, Yufei Liu, Aoxue Zhai, Chufan Zhang, Wai Hin Chui, Zheng Liu, Yingyi Zhang, Nan Liu, Xiang David Li, Keda Zhou, Ning Gao, Bik-Kwoon Tye, Qing Li, Yuanliang Zhai
articles_hidden.abstract: Faithful transmission of chromatin states through cell division requires symmetric transfer of parental histones to daughter strands, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identify the replisome scaffold Ctf4 as a bona fide histone chaperone that directly orchestrates parental histone transfer to preserve epigenetic inheritance. We show that the N-terminal domain (NTD) of Ctf4 harbors a specific histone-binding motif (HBM) embedded within its intrinsically disordered linker region. This HBM engages the DNA-binding surface of histone H3 and, in concert with Spt16 and Mcm2, transiently tethers parental histone hexamer onto Tof1 at the advancing replisome, priming them for subsequent transfer to nascent DNA. Disrupting Ctf4-HBM severely compromises parental histone sequestration, misdirects their recycling away from the lagging strand, and causes substantial loss of gene silencing at heterochromatic loci. Our findings establish Ctf4 not merely as a structural scaffold, but as a central chaperone at the replication fork that actively governs symmetric partitioning of parental histones, thereby ensuring the fidelity of epigenetic memory through successive cell divisions.

articles_hidden.title: Interploidy massively increases meiotic crossovers in pericentromeric recombination deserts
articles_hidden.authors: Loeiz Maillet, Virginie Huteau, Noémie Guiziou, Olivier Coriton, Maryse Taburel-Lodé, Ewen Le Seyec, Matthieu Falque, Olivier Martin, Annaliese S. Mason, Marie Devers, Franz Boideau, Anne-Marie Chèvre, Mathieu Rousseau-Gueutin
articles_hidden.abstract: Meiotic recombination reshuffles genetic diversity through reciprocal DNA exchanges between chromosomes known as crossovers. In most eukaryotes, crossovers are highly constrained in both frequency and distribution, leaving large genomic regions with little or no recombination. A notable exception is the Brassica AAC allotriploid hybrid obtained from a cross between allotetraploid Brassica napus (AACC) and diploid Brassica rapa (AA), which exhibits elevated recombination and crossover formation near centromeres. Here, we generated a CCA allotriploid hybrid from a cross between B. napus and Brassica oleracea (CC), and subsequently produced AAC allotriploids by crossing the CCA hybrid with B. rapa . Both CCA and AAC allotriploids exhibit similar meiotic deregulation, demonstrating that this phenomenon is not restricted to AAC hybrids. Both systems displayed a marked increase in crossover frequency within normally low-recombining chromosome regions, reaching 9.4-fold in AAC and 13.4-fold in CCA allotriploids. Alternating CCA and AAC allotriploids efficiently reshuffled both B. napus subgenomes within only two generations. Using genetic mapping and cytogenetics, we further identified homoeologous exchanges. Remarkably, crossovers occurring on chromosomes involved in homoeologous associations exhibited a more pronounced redistribution toward nonrecombining regions than those on homologously paired chromosomes. Moreover, the frequency of homoeologous associations varied with the diploid progenitor genotype, indicating that genetic factors controlling homoeologous recombination already exist in Brassica diploids. Altogether, our results identify allotriploidy as a simple and powerful strategy to unlock recombination deserts, which harbor 21% of total resistance gene analogs, and provide insights into its potential role in allopolyploid evolution, adaptation, and speciation.

articles_hidden.title: Authentic structure of the CCHFV RNA–nucleoprotein complex at near-atomic resolution
articles_hidden.authors: Zidan Song, Nan Zhang, Fan Wu, Wentao Ni, Yixiao Liu, Dongdong Sun, Bowen Zhang, Jingwu Jian, Wenli Zhao, Xi Wang, Lulu Wang, Hang Shang, Yuhui Wang, Wenming Wang, Zhiyong Lou, Yajie Liu, Zhihong Hu, Zihe Rao, Bo Huang, Yucen Huang, Wei Zheng, Manli Wang, Yu Guo
articles_hidden.abstract: Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) poses a major public health threat without approved vaccines or antivirals. Its ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is essential for replication, but its native architecture and RNA packaging remain elusive. Here, we combine AI-based structural prediction with cryo–electron microscopy to resolve the native structure of the CCHFV RNP purified from CCHFV-infected cells. We report a 3.87 Å structure of a single-turn RNP, and local refinement yielded a 3.55 Å structure of two adjacent NP protomers with continuous RNA. This represents the highest-resolution authentic RNP structure reported among segmented negative-strand RNA viruses (sNSVs), and provides the structural basis for CCHFV RNP assembly. Together with mutational analyses, these findings define the molecular basis of RNA encapsidation and NP oligomerization in the native CCHFV RNP. Our findings provide a hybrid structural framework integrating AI and experimental approaches for understanding genome organization in sNSVs and offer a foundation for future antiviral development.

articles_hidden.title: Phase coding supports neuronal replication and enables combinatorial problem solving
articles_hidden.authors: Hamza Giaffar, Márton Csillag, Zoltan Nadasdy, Dániel Czégel, Eörs Szathmáry
articles_hidden.abstract: Darwinian neurodynamics posits that the brain searches large solution spaces through iterated cycles of variation and selection on competing neural representations. Testing this hypothesis requires a biologically plausible neural replicator: a mechanism that copies spatiotemporal signals faithfully enough to cumulatively improve good solutions, yet loosely enough to allow exploration. We show that phase-coded spike patterns constitute such a replicator. Spike timing referenced to a local field oscillation is compressed into a transferable spike train and reconstructed by coincidence with the receiver’s own field, without synaptic plasticity or a shared code key. As replication noise rises, the system crosses two thresholds. Below the first, faithful copying sustains patterns as dynamic memory. Between the two thresholds, pattern populations evolve. On two hard combinatorial benchmarks, the traveling salesman problem and NK fitness landscapes, neural replication remains competitive with standard search methods at a matched evaluation budget. Beyond the second, an Eigen-like error threshold, inherited information collapses. The network architecture tunes the exploration-exploitation balance: high-degree lattices, where local competition is stronger, exploit smooth landscapes, while low-degree lattices, where weaker competition preserves diversity, search more broadly on rugged landscapes. The framework predicts phase-locked information transfer and phylogenetic structure in replay, as well as a selective loss of combinatorial problem solving beyond the error threshold. These results indicate that a single neurobiological substrate can support memory, variation, and selection, and point to evolutionary dynamics as a candidate computational principle for cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Topological validation of generated scientific images
articles_hidden.authors: Asim K. Dey, Jaidev Goel, Snigdhansu Chatterjee, Yulia R. Gel, H. Vincent Poor
articles_hidden.abstract: Synthetic data have become an indispensable tool for validation, standards development, and product design across a broad range of scientific and engineering disciplines. One of the earliest examples arose in energy systems, where security and confidentiality constraints motivated the development of synthetic power grids and, in turn, novel topological and geometric approaches for evaluating their fidelity. Today, synthetic scientific imagery has emerged as a new critical tool in a variety of applications, ranging from autonomous driving, robotics, and Internet-of-Things technologies to in silico trials, digital twins, and remote sensing of environment. Yet the rigorous assessment of such synthetic images and quantification of their associated uncertainties remains a fundamental challenge. Building on the recent advances in the topological and geometric validation of synthetic power grids, we develop a systematic framework for comparing image data through the persistence of their multiscale shape patterns using the statistical formalism of survival analysis. While the tools of persistent homology and statistical survival analysis are both mature methodologies, they have so far developed largely in isolation. Unlike more traditional comparison methods such as pixel-level similarity or distributional summaries that often fail to capture the complex, multiscale structural characteristics of modern scientific imagery, our approach shows the capability to systematically assess the mismatch between different images at all scales simultaneously, while characterizing the associated uncertainty. The resulting synergistic methodology establishes a broadly applicable statistical topological framework for validating synthetic scientific imagery and, more generally, complex synthetic data products.

articles_hidden.title: Glycosaminoglycans in the structures of Aβ 42 amyloid fibrils purified from mouse brains
articles_hidden.authors: Dev Thacker, Alexander I. P. Taylor, Martin Wilkinson, Felecia Sutton, Jonathan M. Machin, Nayab Fatima, René A. W. Frank, Jessica C. F. Kwok, Neil A. Ranson, Sheena E. Radford
articles_hidden.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has revealed the structures of the ordered cores of amyloid fibrils assembled in vitro and isolated from diseased tissue. Many of the ex vivo amyloid structures contain low-resolution density adjacent to the protein core, often attributed to nonproteinaceous ligands, yet their identity has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize such density in distinct polymorphs of Aβ fibrils purified from the brains of homozygous App NL-F and App NL-G-F knock-in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease. In App NL-G-F fibrils, which are built from the Arctic Aβ variant (E22G), we use immunogold labeling, immunofluorescence microscopy, and cryo-EM to identify the density as the glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate. These GAGs bind to an exposed positively charged patch on the Aβ 42 fibril surface, forming an intimate peptide-GAG copolymer through stacking interactions with the amyloid core. In App NL-F fibrils the predominant polymorph (~ 85% of particles) is glycan-free, with the relevant side chains identified in the App NL-G-F fibrils being buried within the App NL-F fibril core. Formation of the glycan-binding site in a rare polymorph hence involves conformational rearrangement to create the required binding surface. Our findings reveal a structural basis for GAG incorporation into brain-derived amyloid fibrils and highlight amyloid-associated ligands as potential therapeutic targets in protein aggregation disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Wnts are endothelial cell–derived PKD1/PKD2-dependent autocrine/paracrine vasodilators
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich C. Mbiakop, Charles E. MacKay, Alejandro Mata-Daboin, Tessa A. C. Garrud, Roberto Braz Pontes, M. Dennis Leo, Jonathan H. Jaggar
articles_hidden.abstract: Wingless/Int-1 (Wnts) are secreted glycoproteins and canonical Frizzled receptor ligands. Recent evidence indicates that some Wnts can also bind to polycystin 1 (PKD1), a large transmembrane protein which can couple to polycystin 2 (PKD2) to form a nonselective cation channel. The functional significance of PKD1, PKD2, and Wnt-mediated PKD1 signaling in native cell types is poorly understood. Here, we tested the hypothesis that Wnts regulate arterial contractility, investigated the signaling mechanisms and cell types involved, and examined the cellular source of vasoactive Wnts. Our data show that Wnt9b and Wnt5a are endothelial cell (EC)-dependent vasodilators. Wnt9b stimulates vasodilation via EC PKD1/PKD2, whereas Wnt5a acts via both EC PKD1/PKD2 and Frizzled receptors. Wnts stimulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase and small conductance Ca 2+ -activated K + channels in ECs to produce vasodilation. Wnt9b and Wnt5a are present in plasma and intravenous infusion of Wnt9b stimulates an EC PKD1-dependent reduction in systemic blood pressure. Intravascular flow activates angiotensin II type 1 receptors which, through G q/11 and Porcupine signaling, stimulate ECs to secrete Wnt9b and Wnt5a. Wnts which are secreted by ECs in response to flow activate PKD1/PKD2 on ECs and this mechanism contributes to the flow-mediated vasodilation. In summary, we show that Wnts are autocrine/paracrine vasodilator proteins. Intravascular flow stimulates ECs to secrete Wnts, which then act via PKD1/PKD2 and Frizzled receptors on ECs to induce vasodilation.

articles_hidden.title: Localized end-on heating for hot spot ignition in precompressed isochoric plasmas
articles_hidden.authors: Bofang Jiang, Han Xu, Zekun Xu, Bo Zeng, Fuyuan Wu, Ge Zhou, Xiaohu Yang, Qi Zhang, Huanyu Song, Ke Fang, Yihang Zhang, Xiaohui Yuan, Zhe Zhang, Dawei Yuan, Chenglong Zhang, ChuanQi Shi, Zhijie Qiu, Weimin Wang, Xuechun Li, Yutong Li, Jingquan Liu, Jian Zheng, Jianqiang Zhu, Jie Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: In fast ignition inertial confinement fusion, a “heating cone” is employed to shorten the transport distance of the relativistic electron beam (REB) to the high-density plasma core, thereby mitigating energy losses at the plasma edge. However, its insertion depth and survival time are constrained by the sustained pressure from the large-scale plasma edge during the implosion process. Our whole-process simulations demonstrated that, in the double-cone ignition scheme, the head-on collision of two deuterium-tritium plasma jets not only forms a high-density plateau with a small-scale edge, but also substantially reduces the interaction time between the heating cone and the colliding plasma to approximately 0.1 ns . This shortened interaction time enables the heating cone to remain intact after the peak compression, even when placed directly at the small-scale edge of the colliding plasma. The small-scale edge is compatible with the range of the soft-spectrum REB generated by the heating lasers. Such a REB efficiently heats a localized end-on hot spot adjacent to the high-density plateau, guided by a kT-level magnetic field amplified from a seed field during the collision process. Ignited by the localized hot spot, the high-density plateau can undergo sufficient burning and achieve a fusion energy gain of 6.8 using 60 kJ heating lasers.

articles_hidden.title: Vegetation decay enhances terrestrial nitrous acid emissions through nitrate reduction
articles_hidden.authors: Jingwei Zhang, Dianming Wu, Yifei Liu, Yuyao Qin, Shiyang Yu, Jitao Lv, Linqian Li, Wei Li, Chaofan Lian, Haiyan Ran, Lingling Deng, Yi Chen, Ruhai Wang, Zehua Fu, Min Liu, Weili Lin, Chaoyang Xue, Maofa Ge, Yongchun Liu, Weigang Wang, Junling An, Dawei Lu, Markku Kulmala, Qiang Zhang, Gui-Bin Jiang
articles_hidden.abstract: Photolysis of nitrous acid (HONO) drives ozone and secondary aerosol formation, yet its sources remain poorly constrained. We identify HONO emissions from decaying aboveground plant residues as a previously overlooked plant-derived component of terrestrial HONO emissions. Field observations and dual-isotope ( 15 N– 18 O) tracing reveal that HONO arises mainly from nitrate reduction within decomposing plants. We integrated global datasets on vegetation nitrate, litter decomposition, soil, and climate to estimate HONO emissions from vegetation decay at 1.1 ± 0.1 Tg N y −1 . This substantially narrows the long-standing uncertainty in HONO budget. This plant-mediated pathway extends the soil-atmosphere paradigm to soil-plant-atmosphere framework. Moreover, we identify emission hotspots and drivers, assess their climate-driven shifts, and propose region-specific mitigation strategies. These findings uncover a missing link between terrestrial nitrogen cycling and atmospheric reactivity, highlighting biogeochemical controls on air quality.

articles_hidden.title: Gaussian mixture model–based focused refinement for enhanced flexible structure determination in CryoEM and CryoET
articles_hidden.authors: Muyuan Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Dynamic conformational changes of proteins are crucial for their cellular functions. Here we present a unified refinement pipeline for flexible protein structures in both CryoEM and in situ CryoET. Using a Gaussian mixture model–based focused alignment procedure, we improve resolution of small domains in highly dynamic proteins and reveal intricate conformational changes. The method corrects the per-subunit motion of TRPV1 and captures the rotary dynamics of ATP synthase within mitochondria.

articles_hidden.title: Niche constraints drive differences between mycorrhizal fungal guilds in future range shifts
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph D. Edwards, Johan van den Hoogen, Christine V. Hawkes, Mark A. Anthony, Camille S. Delavaux, Justin D. Stewart, Kathleen K. Treseder, Xiao Feng, Monica Papeş, Robert Muscarella, Petr Baldrian, Petr Kohout, E. Toby Kiers, Thomas C. Lauber, Patrick B. Matheny, Thomas W. Crowther, Michael E. Van Nuland, Clara Qin, Colin Averill, Stephanie N. Kivlin
articles_hidden.abstract: Mycorrhizal fungi are a diverse and ubiquitous group of plant symbionts whose distribution strongly influences ecosystem function across the globe. Yet, until now, we do not have quantitative data on the range sizes of different mycorrhizal fungal taxa, limiting our capacity to forecast future shifts in community composition and function. Here, we use 115,924 DNA sequence-derived observations to map the distribution of 651 common mycorrhizal fungal taxa and forecast future changes to their range sizes. We demonstrate that climate, plant cover, and soil factors, particularly mean annual temperature, net primary productivity, and soil organic carbon, exert major control over mycorrhizal fungal distributions. Based on these drivers, the ecological niches of mycorrhizal fungi consistently differ between arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal functional guilds. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal taxa generally occupy a wider niche breadth than ectomycorrhizal fungi, occurring across larger ranges of climate, soil, plant cover, topography, and disturbance conditions. Our models also predict widespread decreases in the suitable range size of mycorrhizal fungal taxa under projected future global climates, with average ranges decreasing by 13.8% or ~2.2 million km 2 under high emissions scenarios (ssp5-8.5). This decrease in projected range size will be most pronounced for ectomycorrhizal fungi, strongly linked to constraints from their smaller overall niches. By generating a global atlas of common mycorrhizal fungi and their associated environmental niche, we establish a critical baseline for widely suspected declines in global fungal biodiversity.

articles_hidden.title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target
articles_hidden.authors: Shohini Ghosh-Choudhary, Jie Liu, Delphine Beaulieu, Ricardo Pineda, Haoxiang Yang, Shria Moturi, Mads B. Larsen, Irene Alfaras, Mehdi Pirooznia, Shihui Liu, Jonathan K. Alder, Yuan Liu, Bill B. Chen, Melanie Königshoff, Toren Finkel
articles_hidden.abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

articles_hidden.title: A decavalent Group B streptococcal biosynthetic conjugate vaccine provides functional immunity to all known serotypes
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel L. Edwards, Kathleen N. McAllister, Isra Darwech, Jenna C. McGuffey, Cory J. Knoot, Nathan Pomper, Lloyd S. Robinson, Anna J. Hooppaw, Stephen Thomas, Kostis Apostolakis, Ashley Shepherd, Stephen Taylor, Paeton L. Wantuch, David A. Rosen, Nichollas E. Scott, Christian M. Harding
articles_hidden.abstract: Globally, 394,000 cases of Group B Streptococcus (GBS) infection occur each year, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Vaccination has emerged as an important strategy to limit GBS infections and disease; however, existing vaccine candidates currently in clinical development do not cover all capsular polysaccharide serotypes. Here, we describe the use of a next generation bioconjugation platform to generate a decavalent GBS vaccine (GBS10V) and characterize its immunological evaluation in animals. Using an evolved PglS bioconjugation platform, capsular polysaccharides from all 10 GBS capsular polysaccharide serotypes were individually expressed and bioconjugated to an optimized Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin A (EPA6) carrier protein engineered with six sequons. Multiple biochemical analyses confirmed the identity of each polysaccharide serotype bioconjugated to EPA6. Moreover, intact mass spectrometry (MS) and MS/MS spectra confirmed the presence of sialic acid in each repeat unit of GBS polysaccharides attached to the carrier, an attribute critical for eliciting an optimal immune response. The GBS10V vaccine was used to immunize outbred CD-1 mice and New Zealand White rabbits with doses of 1, 2, or 5 μg per GBS serotype. Sera analyses demonstrated the GBS10V vaccine induced high serotype-specific immunoglobulin titers to all 10 serotypes. Most importantly, interim and postimmune sera from rabbits demonstrated potent opsonophagocytic killing, with median titers ranging from 646 to 6,145 for all serotypes by day 42. Together, these findings establish GBS10V as a global GBS conjugate vaccine candidate for all patient populations, and thus, justify its further preclinical development.

articles_hidden.title: Universal scaling in the rheology of dense cellular systems
articles_hidden.authors: Helen S. Ansell, Daniel M. Sussman
articles_hidden.abstract: Biological tissues must dynamically transition between solid-like and fluid-like states during processes like morphogenesis and collective migration, often while resisting physiological shear stresses. It remains unclear whether these transitions in tissue dynamics are governed by the same nonequilibrium critical phenomena that control conventional disordered matter. Here we show that the flow response of model cell monolayers under constant shear stress is described by universal scaling behavior, with different flow regimes controlled by the same underlying physical parameters. This framework captures regimes in which the underlying system has both rigid and fluid-like behavior in the absence of imposed fluctuations and stresses. In the rigid regime, small internal fluctuations maintain a solid-like state up to a finite yield stress before the tissue shear thins; the fluid-like regime instead exhibits robust continuous and discontinuous shear thickening. We demonstrate that at high enough stress, the fluid-like regime undergoes structural arrest. This space-filling shear-jamming transition is accompanied by structural changes, including the formation of system-spanning force chains and the emergence of orientational ordering. These results establish confluent tissues as a distinct class of disordered matter, demonstrating that complex nonlinear rheology and structural arrest can emerge entirely through shape-driven topological constraints to regulate biological mechanics.

articles_hidden.title: ZCWPW1 organizes telomeric architecture to drive meiotic chromosome movements
articles_hidden.authors: Wenxin Xie, Manjunath Gowder, Dominic Bazzano, Adrienne Niederriter Shami, Aastha Pandey, Melissa Frasca, Lakshmi Paniker, Luciana Previato de Almeida, Binod Kumar Bharati, Jing Liang, Pankaj Vilas Jadhav, Elizabeth Finn, Attila Tóth, Morgan DeSantis, Jayakrishnan Nandakumar, Evgeny Nudler, Shyamal Mosalaganti, Roberto J. Pezza, Francesca Cole, Saher Sue Hammoud
articles_hidden.abstract: Proper meiotic homolog pairing requires the coordination of two processes: DNA recombination and chromosome-scale mechanical movements. Here, we identify a dual role in both meiotic processes for the chromatin reader ZCWPW1 in mouse spermatocytes. The current dogma proposes that ZCWPW1 acts downstream of PRDM9, reading the PRDM9-deposited H3K4 and K36me3 modifications at recombination hotspots and promoting DSB repair. Using superresolution imaging, we show that ZCWPW1 is diffuse throughout the nucleus but enriched at the nuclear periphery near TRF1, LINC complex components, and dynein. ZCWPW1 CUT&RUN further confirms its genomic enrichment at subtelomeric regions. Loss of ZCWPW1 disrupts telomere architecture, weakens telomere-LINC-motor coupling, and markedly reduces chromosome movement. These defects are more severe than, and mechanistically independent of, those observed in Prdm9 −/− spermatocytes. Together, our data reveal an unexpected PRDM9-independent role for ZCWPW1 as an intranuclear regulator of both recombination and mechanical movements that coordinate to drive efficient homolog pairing.

articles_hidden.title: Language model teams as distributed systems
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Mieczkowski, Katherine M. Collins, Ilia Sucholutsky, Natalia Vélez, Thomas L. Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are growing increasingly powerful. Yet, fundamental constraints on the reasoning, memory, and performance of individual models has sparked recent interest in scaling abilities using LLM teams. With growing deployment of LLM teams at scale, there is a need for principled guidelines for when teams help, how many agents to use, and how structure impacts performance. Rather than building these teams through trial-and-error, we propose using distributed systems as a formal foundation for designing and evaluating LLM teams. Under this formal framework, we derive predictions about how task structure and team architecture should shape performance. Empirical evidence supports these predictions: LLM team scaling follows classical distributed computing laws based on the structure of a task, and centralized and decentralized architectures exhibit the asymmetric vulnerabilities predicted by distributed systems theory. These results establish distributed computing as a generative framework that yields testable, quantitative predictions about LLM team behavior and informs the construction of more efficient and capable teams.

articles_hidden.title: Overlooked biodiversity hotspots revealed by a pluralistic approach for quantifying amphibian biodiscovery needs
articles_hidden.authors: Sky T. Button, Amaël Borzée
articles_hidden.abstract: Undocumented and poorly known species spanning Linnean and Wallacean biodiversity shortfalls pose a major challenge to conservation due to the uncertainty they introduce. To address this, we developed a novel pluralistic approach that accounts for sampling gaps, spatial patterns, environmental associations, and varying conservation needs simultaneously, using amphibians as a case study. Using environment-based richness models and species accumulation curves (SACs), we identified areas with high biodiscovery needs for amphibians. These were concentrated primarily in humid tropical South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and East/Southeast Asia. While environmental models produced more reliable richness estimates than SACs overall, SAC-based estimates nonetheless added unique insights, especially in biodiverse, moderately well-sampled areas like Costa Rica and Panama. By integrating environmental models and SACs—thus leveraging combined strengths of previous approaches—our holistic scoring technique also proved consistent in estimating biodiscovery priorities across ecoregions, enabling robust recommendations for future sampling.

articles_hidden.title: LDHB at the crossroads of diabetes and cognitive dysfunction
articles_hidden.authors: Weikang Cai

articles_hidden.title: Knowledge gaps and scientific progress
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Kedrick, Wenlong Yang, Thomas Gebhart, Yang Wang, Russell J. Funk
articles_hidden.abstract: Knowledge production is often viewed as an endogenous process in which discovery arises through the recombination of existing theories, findings, and concepts. Yet not all recombinations are equally valuable, and identifying those that may prove most generative remains challenging. We propose that a crucial form of recombination occurs when linking concepts creates knowledge gaps—empty regions in the conceptual landscape that may focus scientific attention on unexplored connections. Using computational topology, we develop a method to identify knowledge gaps in science at scale. In this framework, gaps form when new connections complete cycles in evolving networks of scientific concepts. We apply the method to 34,363,623 papers in Microsoft Academic Graph spanning 1900 to 2020. The main analyses use samples ranging from 8,643,571 to 31,983,201 papers. Compared with papers that introduce novel concept pairs without opening gaps, gap-opening papers have greater long-term citation impact, are more disruptive of prior work, and exhibit greater delayed recognition. Gap-opening papers receive fewer citations within five years of publication but more over twenty years, consistent with scientific communities needing time to recognize and develop newly opened research territories. Evidence for the generative capacity of gap-opening papers—as indicated by high citation impact and disruption—replicates in five additional databases (OpenAlex, the PubMed Knowledge Graph, Dimensions, American Physical Society journals, and United States patents) and across eight concept vocabularies, including several derived directly from text. Together, these results point to a distinctive generative role for gap opening in scientific discovery.
