articles_hidden.title: Tumor cell–intrinsic E47 functions as a critical suppressor in antitumor immunity via the FBXL2–PD-L1 axis
articles_hidden.authors: Rongtian Guo, Kun Wang, Jing Xu, Xin Lian, Ruixiao Bai, Xiaoli Chen, Haorui Zheng, Jiexin Gao, Yong Yi, Zhi-Xiong Jim Xiao, Mengmeng Niu
articles_hidden.abstract: The transcription factor E47, encoded by the TCF3 gene, is essential for B and T cell lineage commitment and development. However, whether tumor cell–intrinsic E47 contributes to tumor immunosurveillance remains unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that E47 functions as a critical suppressor of antitumor immunity. Clinical analyses reveal that increased intratumoral TCF3 expression is associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Silencing of E47 in tumor cells markedly inhibits tumor growth, increases infiltration of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, and decreases PD-L1 expression. Mechanistically, E47 transcriptionally represses FBXL2 , which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes PD-L1 polyubiquitination at K270 and proteasomal degradation. Restoration of FBXL2 effectively reverses E47-induced PD-L1 upregulation and tumor growth. Strikingly, Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug nebivolol, an activator of FBXL2, significantly enhances antitumor immunity and improves the efficacy of CTLA-4 blockade therapy in syngeneic tumor mouse models. Together, this study uncovers the E47–FBXL2 axis as a critical pathway governing PD-L1 stability and antitumor immunity, highlighting its therapeutic potential for improving the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: Phosphorylation-dependent ATPase activity regulates subunit shuffling dynamics in cyanobacterial circadian clock proteins
articles_hidden.authors: Tian Yang, Zhuangcheng Zhen, Ying Luan, Yuhai Tu, Qi Ouyang, Yuansheng Cao
articles_hidden.abstract: Protein complexes are essential for cellular functions, with their dynamics increasingly recognized as key regulatory elements. In the cyanobacterial circadian clock, the KaiC hexamer is highly dynamic, undergoing phosphorylation-dependent monomer shuffling that synchronizes individual oscillators. However, the molecular mechanism of monomer shuffling is not fully understood. Here we combine a chromatography-based method with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to quantify subunit exchange in the hexamerization domain of KaiC (KaiC-CI) and in full-length KaiC. We show that ATPase activity is essential for monomer shuffling. Through quantitative modeling of experimental data, we found that adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis at two independent monomer–monomer interfaces disassembles a KaiC-CI hexamer into two oligomers. Two complementary oligomers from two different hexamers can rapidly reform a mixed hexamer. Mechanistically, ATP hydrolysis induces unstable, shuffling-competent states in hexamers, while nucleotide exchange stabilizes them, suppressing shuffling. The balance between these two processes quantitatively explains the relationship between shuffling rate and ATPase activity across KaiC mutants observed in our experiments. Applying this model to full-length KaiC revealed that phosphorylation of the KaiC-CII domain modulates shuffling primarily by affecting the nucleotide exchange rate in the CI domain. This establishes a feedback loop where CII phosphorylation alters CI ATPase activity, which in turn controls subunit exchange to synchronize CII phosphorylation across the KaiC hexamer population. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework linking ATPase-driven subunit exchange to the robustness of circadian clocks, with implications for activation-coupled dynamics in other molecular machines.

articles_hidden.title: NSP1–SAMD9L interactions govern murine rotavirus host range restriction in vivo
articles_hidden.authors: Gaopeng Hou, Mei Ren, Wenhao O. Ouyang, Jiang Tan, Constin Liu, Yinxing Zhu, Qiru Zeng, Yidan Sun, Nicholas C. Wu, Siyuan Ding
articles_hidden.abstract: Rotavirus replication, pathogenesis, and transmission are host-range restricted, yet the viral and host determinants remain poorly defined. Rotavirus nonstructural protein 1 (NSP1) is a multifunctional innate immune antagonist dispensable for replication in permissive cells. Here, using reverse genetics, neonatal mice, intestinal organoids, and comparative proteomics, we identify mouse SAMD9L as a critical host restriction factor selectively antagonized by murine rotavirus-encoded NSP1. An NSP1-deletion murine-like rotavirus produced progeny efficiently in cell lines but was highly attenuated in neonatal mice with no productive intestinal replication, fecal shedding, and diarrhea. Recombinant monoreassortant viruses carrying NSP1 genes from rhesus, bovine, or human rotavirus strains did not support murine intestinal infection, even in Stat1 −/− pups, indicating an additional restriction mechanism beyond STAT1-dependent antiviral signaling. Comparative proteomics identified mouse SAMD9L as a specific interactor of murine NSP1, and NSP1 promoted SAMD9L degradation through a neddylation- and proteasome-dependent pathway. AlphaFold3 guided mutagenesis identified NSP1 residues S364/E366 and SAMD9L residues R455/L462 as functionally important for the NSP1–SAMD9L interaction. Mutations on either side disrupted NSP1–SAMD9L association and prevented SAMD9L degradation. Replication of murine rotaviruses carrying S364A or E366A mutations was undetectable in wild-type mice and was restored in Samd9l −/− mice. Combined deletion of Samd9l and Stat1 permitted replication of otherwise attenuated viruses carrying mismatched NSP1s and enabled fecal IgA seroconversion after a single oral inoculation of Rotarix. These findings identify SAMD9L as a physiologically relevant intestinal restriction factor in mice and show that murine NSP1 antagonism of mouse SAMD9L contributes to murine rotavirus host range restriction in vivo.

articles_hidden.title: Unsupervised Bayesian neural networks enable inference of complex epidemiological and macroevolutionary processes
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriele Marino, Ugnė Stolz, Cecilia Valenzuela Agüí, Tanja Stadler, Daniele Silvestro
articles_hidden.abstract: Birth–death models quantify macroevolutionary and epidemiological processes, including speciation, extinction, and transmission, based on phylogenetic trees. Extensions of these models incorporate external covariates as predictors of these parameters, for instance linking traits or environmental variables with changes in these rates. However, the dependencies between predictors and model parameters are typically restricted to linear, additive effects and may thus fail to capture complex, nonlinear relationships underlying evolutionary dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose a framework that leverages unsupervised Bayesian neural networks to flexibly model functional relationships between these parameters and a broad set of predictors, including categorical traits, quantitative variables, and time series data. Based on these covariates, the network weights and thus the resulting birth–death dynamics are estimated jointly with the phylogenetic tree, obtained directly from sequence alignment data. Extensive simulations show that this approach accurately recovers predictor–parameter relationships, mitigates overfitting, and remains robust across both macroevolutionary and epidemiological contexts. Using explainable AI, we further show that our framework reliably identifies the most influential predictors and yields interpretable descriptions of their impact on the inferred rates. Finally, we apply our method in two empirical analyses: linking SARS-CoV-2 migration dynamics with travel data during its early spread in Europe, and inferring trait- and time-dependent speciation and extinction rates in the diversification of platyrrhines. Our framework substantially expands the capabilities of birth–death models, providing a powerful and flexible approach to infer complex epidemiological and macroevolutionary processes.

articles_hidden.title: Lipid-induced Caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking is associated with lipid droplet growth
articles_hidden.authors: Esther Ocket, Tamara Pietrucik, Luis Wong-Dilworth, Daniel Aik, Michaela Rath, Dmytro Puchkov, Max Ruwolt, Martin Lehmann, Claudia Matthaeus
articles_hidden.abstract: Caveolae are 50 to 100 nm sized plasma membrane invaginations involved in cellular lipid uptake and lipid accumulation. Several caveolin1 and cavin1 mutations are associated with human lipodystrophy. Previous research identified caveolae proteins at lipid droplets, although their specific cellular function at lipid droplets is not understood. Here, we show that extracellular dietary lipids like oleic acid and cholesterol shift caveolae at the plasma membrane to highly spherical invaginations and induce the internalization of caveolin1. Within 3 h of lipid treatment, caveolin1 accumulates specifically to lipid droplets. Correlative fluorescence Focused Ion Beam – Scanning Electron Microscopy and split-APEX proteomics revealed that this localization occurs in the absence of intact caveolar vesicles but caveolin1 alone. Mechanistically, caveolin1 trafficking to lipid droplets is regulated by EHD2 at the plasma membrane, is dynamin independent, and proceeds via EEA1- and Rab5-positive endosomes within 1 h of oleic acid treatment. Lipid droplet accumulation of caveolin1 is independent of lysosomal activity. Functionally, caveolin1-enriched lipid droplets exhibit a significant increase in size, demonstrating that caveolin1 is critical for lipid droplet growth. Notably, the deletion of the central caveolin1 β-barrel (Cav1-F160X), a mutation identified in lipodystrophy patients, abolished caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking and lipid droplet growth. Taken together, our results show that dietary lipids trigger caveolin1 internalization and accumulation at lipid droplets and a caveolin1-dependent lipid droplet growth, thereby providing an initial mechanistic basis for the lipodystrophic phenotype associated with caveolin1 mutations.

articles_hidden.title: Harness design matters for AI capabilities in mathematics
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammed Abouzaid, Nikhil Srivastava, Rachel Ward, Lauren Williams
articles_hidden.abstract: To assess the ability of current AI systems to correctly solve research-level mathematics problems, we tested four AI systems on a set of ten problems in a broad range of mathematical fields; these problems arose naturally in the research process of the contributors. This document includes our methodology, and the results of our testing, including the assessment of human reviewers and a report of costs. We provide links to supplementary documents including the human solutions, the AI-generated solutions, and the referee reports and logs for the AI-generated solutions.

articles_hidden.title: Reply to Kochiyama et al.: Extensive inferred overlap in cognitive abilities complicate evolutionary models of Neanderthal replacement

articles_hidden.title: PRMT5 licenses AARS1-dependent histone lactylation to amplify microglial glycolytic reprogramming in neuropathic pain
articles_hidden.authors: Honghao Song, Tong Hua, Lei Peng, Xiaoyi Fan, Yutong Yang, Rongrong Fan, Li Cao, Chaofeng Han, Hongbin Yuan
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuropathic pain involves persistent metabolic and transcriptional remodeling in spinal microglia, but the mechanisms linking these processes remain unclear. Time-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing after chronic constriction injury identified increased PRMT5 expression in glycolysis-enriched activated microglia. Microglia-specific Prmt5 deletion or pharmacological inhibition reduced glycolytic remodeling and pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, PRMT5 associated with alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1), promoted AARS1-associated symmetric dimethylation and nuclear accumulation, and supported AARS1-dependent H3K18la and H4K12la. Disrupting AARS1 nuclear localization impaired histone lactylation and glycolytic responses. The pathway was validated in primary microglia, spinal microglia, and female mice. Chromatin profiling linked injury-associated histone lactylation to glycolytic gene programs. Finally, biomimetic siPRMT5 nanoparticles preferentially reduced PRMT5 in spinal microglia and alleviated pain hypersensitivity. These findings identify a PRMT5–AARS1–histone lactylation pathway that reinforces microglial glycolytic reprogramming and represents a potential therapeutic target for neuropathic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Rural outdoor air pollution exceeds urban levels in the Delhi megacity region
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Joseph Campmier, Sofiya Rao, Amarendra Singh, Saumya Singh, María Teresa Hernández, Nidhi Malik, Swagata Dey, Ajay Pillarisetti, Kalpana Balakrishnan, Sagnik Dey, Joshua S. Apte
articles_hidden.abstract: India routinely experiences some of the highest concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) air pollution in the world. Although India’s population predominantly lives in rural areas and smaller cities, policy efforts to date have emphasized air pollution in India’s large cities. In contrast, there is limited understanding of air pollutant dynamics in India’s rural and less urbanized areas. Here, we established a well-calibrated lower-cost PM 2.5 sensor network spanning a wide range of urbanicity (population densities: 300 to 30,000 people/km 2 ) outside and inside of Delhi. The network of 49 sites incorporated a 160 km measurement transect to capture ambient PM 2.5 trends of the Delhi megacity, as well as stratified measurements in villages, small cities, and Delhi itself. We report on data from 5 mo of operation (July–November 2024) spanning the cleanest and most polluted times of the year. PM 2.5 concentrations at rural sites consistently exceeded those at urban sites by about 20% during every month of our study. Analysis of diurnal PM 2.5 cycles showed sharp morning (approximately 06:00–10:00 LT) and evening (approximately 16:00–20:00 LT) concentration peaks at rural sites that were absent at urban sites. We attribute these events to widespread use of solid fuels for cooking, heating, and small-scale industry in suburban and rural settings. These striking enhancements in rural air pollution are missed by satellite remote sensing data, and our findings run contrary to the general societal perception that Indian cities are pollution hotspots relative to rural areas.

articles_hidden.title: Structural and biochemical impact of clinically relevant constitutively active parathyroid hormone receptor 1 mutations
articles_hidden.authors: Isabella C. Russell, Elita Yuliantie, Zamara Mariam, Hariprasad Venogupal, George Christopoulos, Xin Zhang, Brian P. Cary, Christopher Phillips, Arjan Snijder, Taianá Maia de Oliveira, Giuseppe Deganutti, Matthew J. Belousoff, Patrick M. Sexton, Denise Wootten
articles_hidden.abstract: Parathyroid hormone receptor 1 (PTH1R) constitutively active mutants, including H223 2.50 R and T410 6.42 P, are responsible for Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, a form of short-limbed dwarfism. Here, we expand pharmacological understanding and present cryoelectron microscopy structures of the constitutively active PTH1R mutants, H223 2.50 K, H223 2.50 R, and T410 6.42 P, in complex with Gs protein and PTH(1–34), and H223 2.50 R and T410 6.42 P in the ligand free Gs complexed form. These reveal modifications in polar networks that allow for constitutive G protein coupling and subsequent signaling. In the absence of a peptide bound to the extracellular side of the PTH1R, TM6 adopts a distinct conformation relative to the PTH(1–34) bound wild-type PTH1R coupled with Gs. Combined with molecular dynamics analysis of inactive and Gs bound receptors, this work reveals distinct mechanisms that lead to differing receptor activation states and consequently promote distinct constitutive activity and agonist-mediated pharmacological profiles.
