articles_hidden.abstract: Quantum phenomena can be exploited to tackle certain problems beyond the reach of classical approaches. In this study, we focus on coordinated decision-making among many players without communication, the study of which, on current quantum processors, has remained elusive. Using a superconducting qubit processor, we show that quantum contextuality enables certain tasks to be performed with success probabilities beyond classical limits. With a few qubits, we illustrate quantum contextuality with the magic square game and quantify it through a Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality violation. To examine many-body contextuality, we implement the N -player Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger game and separately solve a two-dimensional hidden linear function problem, advancing the state of the art on fidelity and system size in both tasks. Our work introduces benchmarking of quantum processors using contextuality-based algorithms.

articles_hidden.title: Divergent activation of the RXFP1 relaxin receptor by protein and small-molecule agonists
articles_hidden.authors: James Osei-Owusu, Tristan Girbau, Xunan Wang, Jeffrey S. Smith, Pengxiang Shen, Sarah C. Erlandson, Amanda K. Williamson, Xiaojing Cong, Mark W. Grinstaff, Daniel E. Kahne, Cherine Bechara, Andrew C. Kruse
articles_hidden.abstract: The relaxin receptor RXFP1 is a therapeutic target owing to its potential benefits in the treatment of fibrosis and heart failure. Protein and small-molecule agonists are currently in midstage clinical trials for various forms of heart disease. In this work, we present three cryo–electron microscopy structures of RXFP1: ligand-free, bound to the native agonist relaxin-2, and bound to the small-molecule drug candidate AZD5462. These structures reveal that relaxin-2 engages the receptor’s ectodomain, whereas AZD5462 binds to the transmembrane domain. Together with hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, we show that relaxin-2 induces reorganization of the linker domain into a helical secondary structure. By contrast, AZD5462 stabilizes an active conformation through a distinct set of conformational rearrangements. Altogether, our findings define divergent activation mechanisms for protein and small-molecule agonists of RXFP1.

articles_hidden.title: Molecular adhesion for durable metal halide perovskite modules
articles_hidden.authors: Chenglin Yang, Tian Hou, Yafeng Xu, Charles Robinson, Joshua S. Stein, Yingtong Guo, Qingchao Chang, Hong Li, Lang Yu, Yuanyuan Qin, Omar F. Mohammed, Yuelong Huang, Shuai You, Xiaopeng Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: Reliable, strong, and low-loss interfaces are needed for durable perovskite photovoltaics. We have developed a molecular interface layer with an aromatic dual-site-binding ligand to improve the reliability of perovskite modules. The buried interface was strengthened through intermolecular interactions between the ligand and hole-selective layer and through strong chemical bonds. The resulting heterointerface enhances perovskite adhesion and releases interface strain, making the device more resilient to thermomechanical stresses. This device architecture achieves a power conversion efficiency of 22.7% for 900–square centimeter (cm 2 ) submodules (aperture area: 655 cm 2 ) and 21.3% for 7200-cm 2 standard modules (aperture area: 6380 cm 2 ). The champion 7200-cm 2 standard module maintained consistent performance during 105 days of outdoor testing, as independently measured by the Photovoltaic Accelerator for Commercializing Technologies (PACT) center.

articles_hidden.title: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects
articles_hidden.authors: Dylan G. E. Gomes, Lisa G. Crozier, James J. Ruzicka, David D. Huff, Joshua D. Stewart
articles_hidden.abstract: Pacific salmon are depleted due to anthropogenic impacts, and populations have failed to recover despite management interventions. Predation on salmon by pinnipeds and seabirds has been suggested as a barrier to recovery, leading to calls for predator culls by some. However, no studies have evaluated the whole-ecosystem impact of removing these predators nor estimated the direct and indirect effects of these culls on salmon. We use an end-to-end ecosystem model to assess the efficacy of widespread culls in marine environments. We find that culls are unlikely to benefit salmon due to the indirect food web effects of predator reduction and the low biomass of top predator groups. Instead, more abundant fish predators, northward-expanding competitors, and temperature-sensitive prey have larger effects on salmon in the ocean.

articles_hidden.title: Telemetric calorimetry for wireless continuous reaction profiling
articles_hidden.authors: Sukwoo Lee, Evan A. Weingarten, Michael F. Reynolds, Kevin Sun, Alejandro J. Cortese, Huw M. L. Davies, Alyosha C. Molnar, Paul L. McEuen, Song Lin
articles_hidden.abstract: Real-time monitoring of chemical reactions is often achieved with specialized instrumentation along with custom-designed reactors or intrusive sampling. In this study, we introduce reaction telemetry, a wireless analytical strategy that enables remote, nonintrusive monitoring directly within operating reaction vessels. This approach uses light-powered microelectronic devices that communicate optically and function as autonomous sensing elements. We demonstrate continuous calorimetric measurements across diverse chemical reactions relevant to pharmaceutical and fine chemical synthesis, including photochemical and electrochemical systems, providing access to reaction kinetics under native operating conditions with subsecond temporal resolution. The resulting measurements will support catalyst evaluation, safety assessment, and mechanistic investigation and will accelerate data-driven reaction discovery. By embedding analytical functionality directly within reaction vessels, reaction telemetry establishes a general framework for information-rich observation of chemical processes across research, development, and education.

articles_hidden.title: The fate of poised pre-mRNAs shapes mitochondrial activity and cellular differentiation
articles_hidden.authors: Xavier Rambout, Rina Nagao, Victor Gu, Sophie Werner, Justin Youngyunpipatkul, Jadon Schlierf, Christoph Pröschel, Lynne E. Maquat
articles_hidden.abstract: Although RNA quality control tightly regulates gene expression, the scope of its regulatory functions in the nucleus remains unclear. In this study, we describe the quality control, on chromatin, of poised intron–containing polyadenylated RNAs (PIA-RNAs). Whether these precursor messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) constitute immature mRNAs whose splicing is pending or, alternatively, are degraded by the nuclear RNA exosome depends on whether they engage nuclear cap-binding protein 3 (NCBP3) or anillin, respectively. Many PIA-RNAs inversely controlled by NCBP3 and anillin encode mitochondrial factors. Thus, NCBP3 depletion in mouse as well as pathogenic mutations in the RNA exosome in humans result in reduced mitochondrial activity, muscle weakness, cerebellar hypomyelination, and diminished motor coordination. Our findings reveal a competition between pre-mRNA metabolic pathways whose balance controls mitochondrial function and, when perturbed, leads to neurological diseases.

articles_hidden.title: Balancing redox-mediated cytotoxicity and catalysis in natural product biosynthesis
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah A. Boesger, Emma Fang, Rongbin Wang, Ralph J. Harte, Arina Koroleva, Taylan Tunckanat, Areeba N. Momin, Sean J. Elliott, Mikko Metsä-Ketelä, Sean A. Newmister, David H. Sherman
articles_hidden.abstract: Redox-mediated chemistry is central to both the biosynthesis and cytotoxicity of many natural products, yet how microbes balance these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a conserved mechanism that coordinates three redox-mediated processes in secondary metabolite biosynthesis: self-protection, prevention of substrate degradation, and late-stage biosynthesis. Using the antitumor antibiotic doxorubicin as a model system, we show that the vicinal oxygen chelate (VOC) protein DnrV prevents reactive oxygen species formation and substrate degradation while promoting P450 catalysis. We expand this paradigm to a conserved family of VOC-fold proteins, redox-associated cytotoxin-binding proteins (REACT), found across bacteria, fungi, and plants. REACT represents a multifunctional protein class that balances antibiotic assembly, self-protection, and prevention of metabolite destruction, providing a foundational understanding of production of redox-active natural products.

articles_hidden.title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Maria Borruto, Tabea Kohlund, Lukas Rettig, Martin von Renesse, Christian Alexander Hammer, Nikolas Leonhardt, Barbara Kurpiers, Claudia Calpe-López, Luca Benn, Hans-Christoph Friederich, Thomas Kuner, Rainer Spanagel, Sebastian Wieland
articles_hidden.abstract: Childhood adversity increases the risk of chronic pain and anxiety later in life, particularly in women, yet the neural mechanisms linking early-life stress to adult vulnerability remain elusive. Here, we show that social isolation and nerve injury interact to amplify activity-dependent synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the paraventricular thalamus-to–central amygdala pathway in female, but not male, mice. This female-specific circuit sensitization enhances mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance behaviors in adulthood. Chemogenetic pathway inhibition selectively rescued these behaviors when stress and injury co-occurred, whereas sustained and phasic pathway activation triggered mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance, respectively. Together, these findings uncovered a latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state that is unmasked by a subsequent injury and transforms early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

articles_hidden.title: Quaternary carbon–guided carbocation cascade rearrangement to enantioenriched polycycles
articles_hidden.authors: Xu-Dong Hu, Yu-Qing Zheng, Ke Zhai, Tang-Yuan Li, Zhi-Xin Guo, Jian-Ling Li, Wen-Bo Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Polycyclic frameworks are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, yet their efficient enantioselective synthesis remains a longstanding challenge. Carbocation cascade cyclization is a textbook reaction that has transformed the synthesis of fused polycycles, but extending this strategy to bridged architectures requires precise control over highly reactive carbocation intermediates while overcoming the intrinsic energetic barrier of transannular cyclization. Herein, we report a quaternary-carbon-guided carbocation cascade rearrangement platform that enables enantioselective and divergent assembly of complex polycyclic architectures from readily available substrates. An enantioenriched quaternary center, installed via transition-metal-catalyzed allylation, serves as a temporary structural linchpin in an acid-triggered cationic cascade rearrangement process, forming multiple bonds and chiral centers in a single step. In combination with pre-embedded quaternary centers, this strategy provides bicyclic and bridged polycyclic frameworks bearing multiple stereocenters with high enantioselectivity.

articles_hidden.title: Interpenetrating bottlebrush elastomer for low-loss soft ultrasonic interfaces
articles_hidden.authors: Shu Wang, Runze Li, Zihan Tang, Ying Li, Chen Gong, Won Jun Song, Chwee Teck Lim, Xiaodong Chen, Xuanhe Zhao
articles_hidden.abstract: Ultrasound imaging relies on soft interfaces that transmit sound efficiently between a device and the body. Conventional gel couplants provide low acoustic loss but contain mobile liquid phases that can dry, flow, or leach during extended use. By contrast, mobile phase–free elastomers are more stable but generally attenuate megahertz ultrasound strongly, limiting their use as couplants. We report an interpenetrating bottlebrush elastomer molecularly designed to overcome this trade-off. A densely grafted backbone lowers the shear modulus without increasing shear loss, whereas well-packed sidechains reduce bulk compressibility, jointly suppressing acoustic attenuation in a soft elastomer. The resulting elastomer combines soft tissue–like mechanics with low-loss acoustics, providing a durable couplant for soft ultrasonic interfaces.

articles_hidden.title: Angular momentum transfer from an optical vortex to an atomic rotor
articles_hidden.authors: Yu-Lung Tang, Ryan Tollefsen, Neha Yadav, Michael W. Zuerch, Hartmut Häffner
articles_hidden.abstract: Light carries angular momentum in two forms: spin, associated with polarization, and orbital, associated with helical wavefronts. Whereas spin angular momentum underlies well-known atomic selection rules, the role of orbital angular momentum (OAM) in light-matter interaction continues to be discussed in the literature. In this work, we investigate OAM transfer from a vortex laser beam to a trapped-ion quantum rotor using rotational sidebands of the electric quadrupole transition of 40 Ca + . We directly observe coherent transfer of optical OAM into quantized rotation and identify distinct selection rules for different rotational sidebands. This observation provides experimental evidence for a scale-dependent separation of angular momentum transfer pathways in light-matter interactions. Further, our work elucidates the previously reported modified selection rules in trapped-ion experiments, establishing a unified framework for twisted light–matter interactions.

articles_hidden.title: Quiet within, chaos without: Turbulence shelters drive selective particle capture and release
articles_hidden.authors: Matteo Sabato, Sarah Chong, Yaocheng Li, Zhe Xu, Daqian Gao, Martin J. Falk, Stefano Sacanna, William T. M. Irvine
articles_hidden.abstract: Turbulence is chaotic, yet its fluctuations follow a structured, nonequilibrium energy cascade unconstrained by the equilibrium theorems that limit passive energy extraction from molecular gases. Here, we introduce turbulence shelters: hollow shells with a single aperture that filter eddies by scale, sustaining gradients in fluctuation intensity that drive directional particle transport despite zero mean fluid flux. Across three orders of magnitude in size, shelters establish particle concentration contrasts between their interior and the surrounding flow, with selectivity controlled by particle geometry, inertia, thermal fluctuations, and electrostatic forces. At the microscale, shelters discriminate particles differing by tens of nanometers independently of material composition. These results establish a design principle for selective filtration: Geometry that compartmentalizes turbulent fluctuations can harness ambient eddies to direct particle transport.

articles_hidden.title: Meso–microporous zeolitic materials with thin walls containing ordered 10-ring channels
articles_hidden.authors: Zhenghan Zhang, Jiazheng Sun, Chao Ma, Xudong Tian, Mao Luo, Qike Jiang, Lei Han, Cong Lin, Haitao Song, Le Xu, Wei Lin, Jian Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Aluminosilicate zeolites offer exceptional size and shape selectivity but suffer from diffusion limitations imposed by subnanometer micropores. Intrinsically meso–microporous zeolites integrate mesopores with micropores to create interconnected pathways that accelerate diffusion while preserving selectivity, yet their synthesis remains challenging. In this study, we report NJU120-5 and NJU120-7, intrinsically meso–microporous aluminosilicates that integrate micropores with mesopores enclosed by two-T-atom-thick walls containing 10-ring channels, forming a fully interconnected three-dimensional pore network. Their plausible framework models were established on the basis of advanced electron ptychographic imaging, revealing representative quasi-rectangular mesopores in calcined NJU120-5 with a uniform width of ~12 angstroms and lengths from 41 to 162 angstroms. Both materials exhibit high porosity, strong Brønsted acidity, and enhanced performance in heavy-oil cracking, delivering high yields of valuable fuels with suppressed coke formation.

articles_hidden.title: A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander B. Silva, Matthew K. Leonard, Patrick W. Hullett, Deborah F. Levy, Catherine Wang, Duo Xu, Ilina Bhaya-Grossman, Edward F. Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Wernicke’s area in the posterior temporal lobe is classically defined by its role in speech comprehension, yet a paradox remains: Why does damage here also profoundly impair speech production? Using direct human brain recordings, cortical stimulation, and lesion analysis, we found that this region is not solely for perception. A discrete subzone within Wernicke’s area, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), becomes active before speech, is causally necessary for speech production, and codes features of whole upcoming words rather than low-level acoustics or articulatory information. Its neural activity is distinct from the auditory-feedback responses nearby and can decode intended speech in people with paralysis. Thus, while Wernicke’s area is a key part of auditory cortex, it contains a dedicated subregion for speech generation.

articles_hidden.title: A DNA Typewriter records the cell lineage history of a mouse, from zygote to late organogenesis
articles_hidden.authors: Qi Yu, Haedong Kim, Sophie Seidel, James F. Acosta-Clark, Beth K. Martin, Kyle O’Connor, Riza M. Daza, Molly Gasperini, Jenny F. Nathans, Maggie Lam, Elena Gamo, Shruthi VijayKumar, Lauren Kuo, Jean-Benoît Lalanne, Kamen P. Simeonov, Marion Pepper, Cole Trapnell, Jesse M. Gray, Junhong Choi, Chengxiang Qiu, Jay Shendure
articles_hidden.abstract: Mammalian biology unfolds over time, within tissues and organs opaque to our eyes and instruments. We applied DNA Typewriter, a sequential molecular recorder, to record the cell lineage of a mouse over nearly 2 weeks of development. From one embryo, we reconstructed a time-calibrated, parsimony-supported, zygote-rooted phylogeny of 1.28 million transcriptionally profiled cells. A burst of editing unequivocally marks the daughters of the first cleavage, which serve as inline replicates. We quantified clonal dominance arising during gastrulation. Tree siblings share cell type far above chance; heterotypic siblings mark terminal differentiations. Temporal sweeps of clade co-occurrence recover a dated hierarchy of cell type couplings; imputed labels for internal nodes recapitulate known state paths. A lineage-anchored ontogeny of mammalian development, long out of reach, is coming into view.

articles_hidden.title: Ribosome-associated vesicles promote activity-dependent local translation in neurons
articles_hidden.authors: Eva Martin-Solana, Stephen D. Carter, Karthik Krishnamurthy, Giovanni de Nola, Jiying Ning, Jill R. Glausier, Matias A. Preisegger, Laura Harris, Lauren Meyer, Leanna Eisenman, Paul N. Joseph, Cedric Bouchet-Marquis, Ken Wu, Catherina L. Mobini, Amber N. Frantz, Stephanie Puig, Cheri M. Hampton, Nadine Kabbani, David Mankus, Eric K. F. Donahue, Kristopher Burkewitz, Grant J. Jensen, Simon C. Watkins, Karl Deisseroth, Lief E. Fenno, Michael S. Gold, Zachary P. Wills, Abigail K. R. Lytton-Jean, Sulagna Das, Zachary Freyberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Local protein synthesis in axons and dendrites underpins synaptic plasticity. However, the composition of the protein synthesis machinery in distal neuronal processes and the mechanisms for its deployment to local translation sites remain unclear. Here, we employed multi-scale imaging that combines cryo-electron tomography, volume electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging to identify endoplasmic reticulum-derived KDEL-positive vesicles, a subset of which are decorated with ribosomes (Ribosome-Associated Vesicles, RAVs) in neurites. We demonstrate that neuronal stimulation triggers compartment-specific responses: dendrites accumulate stationary KDEL-positive vesicles at sites of enhanced translation, while axons accelerate vesicle transport. cLTP stimulation additionally increases the proportion of KDEL-positive vesicles that carry ribosomes, expanding the local RAV pool. Real-time imaging of translation at single mRNA resolution reveals that RAV-associated translation sites exhibit ∼30% greater nascent-peptide signal amplitude compared to periods without RAV association, indicating that RAVs boost local translation output. These findings establish RAVs as specialized platforms that integrate activity-dependent signals with local protein synthesis, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how neurons achieve precise spatiotemporal control of translation.

articles_hidden.title: Clearance of erythrocytes after subarachnoid hemorrhage: Cranial lymphatic and dural pathways
articles_hidden.authors: Tangtang Xiang, Elliot Norris, Sarmad Peymaei, Diego Ulisse Pizzagalli, Steven T. Proulx
articles_hidden.abstract: The clearance of toxic blood products from the brain after subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is critical for neurological recovery, yet the precise anatomical pathways and cellular mechanisms responsible for this process remain poorly defined. Using murine models of both arterial perforation and low-rate intracisternal injection, we have mapped a comprehensive, multifaceted network of red blood cell (RBC) distribution and clearance. We found that, while RBCs accessed peripheral lymphatic vessels via cranial nerves, an extensive distribution of extravasated erythrocytes could also be observed sequestered within nonendothelial, collagen-lined interstitial channels flanking the major dural venous sinuses. By day 2 post-SAH, regional macrophages actively cleared some trapped erythrocytes. These findings provide a detailed spatiotemporal framework of SAH blood clearance, revealing promising anatomical and cellular targets to accelerate stroke recovery.

articles_hidden.title: Recovery and resurrection of chiral homogeneous catalysts for closed-loop recycling
articles_hidden.authors: Shiqi Liu, Najwa Arafah, Jingjun Huang, Etienne A. LaPierre, Darby E. H. Curtis, Jiajing Li, Jolene P. Reid, Thibaud Bregent, Stellios Arseniyadis, David C. Leitch
articles_hidden.abstract: Homogeneous catalysis by transition metal complexes is essential for chemical synthesis; however, these processes remain unsustainable because the catalysts are generally not recovered. We address this problem with a framework for closed-loop catalyst recycling. This approach centers on two chemical processes: stasis, where catalytic activity is selectively halted while retaining molecular integrity; and anastasis, where full catalytic function is restored. We apply this framework to recycle chiral palladium catalysts used for asymmetric allylic alkylation. ortho -Quinone oxidants drive the catalyst to converge on a discrete Pd II complex that is readily recovered, while mild reductants regenerate active Pd 0 precatalysts in a subsequent step. By rendering catalyst deactivation, isolation, and reactivation chemically addressable, this work is an important step toward circular, resource-efficient synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: TRIM28-mediated SUMOylation of ERG at K389 conveys PARP inhibitor resistance by inhibiting 53BP1 expression in CRPC
articles_hidden.authors: Shiwei Liu, Zhe Hong, Zhongyuan Wang, Yongqing Zhang, Chenye Jiang, Yuchen Jiang, Runkai Zhang, Zheng Liu, Zhi Shang, Guowen Lin, Zongyuan Hong, Bo Dai
articles_hidden.abstract: Both intrinsic and acquired resistance to poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPis) have emerged as a formidable challenge in clinical practice. Here, we report that the transcription factor E-twenty-six (Ets)-related gene ( ERG ) was highly expressed in PARPi-resistant prostate cancer and was correlated with PARPi resistance in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) cells. ERG was posttranslationally modified by tripartite motif-containing 28 (TRIM28) as SUMOylation at lysine 389 (K389), which promotes DNA homologous recombination repair (HRR), thereby weakening the efficacy of PARPis. Mechanistically, the SUMOylation of ERG (K389) inhibited protein degradation mediated by the SPOP-mediated ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, thereby stabilizing the protein. Concurrently, this posttranslational modification increased HRR capacity by inhibiting 53BP1 expression, which in turn reduced PARPi sensitivity. Blockade of ERG K389 SUMOylation can effectively impair DNA repair efficacy and overcome PARPi resistance. These findings suggest that TRIM28-mediated ERG SUMOylation conveys resistance to PARPis by inhibiting 53BP1 expression; combined TRIM28/ERG targeting and PARPi therapy may improve outcomes for ERG-positive CRPC patients.

articles_hidden.title: PEG-free tunable poly(2-oxazoline) lipids modulate mRNA-LNP biodistribution and expression in vivo
articles_hidden.authors: Colin Basham, Matt Haney, Yuling Zhao, Hallie Hutsell, Reb Kornahrens, Liubov Palchak, Konstantin A. Lukyanov, Kyoungtea Kim, Ayse Baysal, Michael C. Brown, Alexander V. Kabanov, Jacob D. Ramsey
articles_hidden.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed drug delivery, enabling the stabilization and efficient intracellular delivery of nucleic acids. Current LNP platforms, including those used in clinical COVID-19 vaccines, rely on polyethylene glycol (PEG) to stabilize the nanoparticle. However, anti-PEG antibodies are ubiquitous in the population and are a major cause of anaphylaxis and reduced therapeutic efficacy by accelerating the blood clearance of PEGylated products. Here, we report the development of poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) lipids as alternatives. POx polymers are poorly immunogenic and mitigate accelerated blood clearance. Upon varying polymer hydrophilicity and molecular weight, we screened transfection efficiency in multiple cell lines and evaluated top candidates in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that POx-lipids incorporating short hydrophilic oxazoline chains enhance target transfection while mitigating liver expression. These POx-lipids boost expression in key extrahepatic tissues, including lymph nodes and spleen. This marks a notable advancement toward replacing PEG in LNP therapies and provides a clear path to optimizing POx-lipids for targeted vaccine and therapeutic applications.

articles_hidden.title: Psychedelics shift decision strategies and reconfigure orbitofrontal dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: C. Delgado-Sallent, S. A. Ahmed, A. Khawaja-Lopez, B. S. Lee, U. Mishra, R. A. Senne, S. Ramirez, B. B. Scott
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood. To address this, we trained mice on a free-response perceptual decision-making task that disentangles bias-driven from sensory-guided strategies. Acute administration of psilocybin or ketamine slowed decision times while improving accuracy. Behavioral modeling combining drift diffusion and GLM-HMM approaches revealed that these effects were driven by increased decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states. Whole-brain c-Fos mapping identified modulation of distributed task-related networks, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Calcium imaging showed that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations. Together, these findings indicate that psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics, providing a system-level account of their effects on perceptual decisions.

articles_hidden.title: In vivo screening reveals new regulators of natural killer cell development and functional response to acute cytomegalovirus infection
articles_hidden.authors: Eleanor J. Pring, Simon Clare, Roseanna Hare, Sam Sheppard, Morgan Marsden, INTREPID consortium, Mathew Clement, Lucy Chapman, Katherine Harcourt, Carmen Ballesteros Reviriego, Cordelia Brandt, Agnieszka Andres, Bushra Abu-Helil, Vivek Iyer, Louise van der Weyden, Maria A. Oliver, Paul A. Lyons, Eddie C. Y. Wang, David J. Adams, Matthew C. Cook, Daniel M. Davis, Ian R. Humphreys, Anneliese O. Speak
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells are critical innate immune effectors in antiviral and antitumor responses. However, the factors governing NK cell development and function remain incompletely understood. To address this, we adopted an in vivo screening approach, generating a panel of mice deficient in genes differentially expressed across NK cell maturation stages or following viral infection. We performed a combinational screen comprising baseline immunophenotyping and mouse cytomegalovirus (MCMV) challenge. We identified regulators of NK cell development, including transcriptional regulators and proteins with putative trafficking functions. MCMV challenge studies additionally identified proteins that affected antiviral immunity independently of NK cell phenotypes, including a previously undescribed regulator of NK cell degranulation, synaptotagmin-like protein 3. Identified genes exhibited a trend toward reduced tolerance to loss of function in large-scale human sequencing studies and evidence for reduced NK cell numbers in a cohort of patients with immunodeficiency. Together, these findings provide a resource of NK-expressed genes important for NK cell maturation and function, with relevance to human health.

articles_hidden.title: A supergene converts queen-destined larvae into a novel caste in ants
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel V. Arsenault, Géraldine Bienvenu, Christina M. Daly, Waring Trible
articles_hidden.abstract: Novel morphological castes are a major source of phenotypic diversity in ants, but their genetic and developmental origins remain unresolved. Here we identify ergatoid , a 6.5-megabase dominant supergene that is necessary and sufficient to generate a novel caste in an undescribed species of moss ant, Leptothorax AF-erg . The resulting wingless (ergatoid) queens represent a distinct morphological population intermediate between workers and the ancestral winged queen caste. Morphometric and genotyping analyses show that ergatoid produces this caste by modifying queen-destined larvae rather than altering worker development or generating a new larval population. Transcriptomic and candidate gene analyses most strongly support altered ecdysone signaling and reduced insulin signaling as the developmental basis for this phenotype. These results show that a single large-effect genetic element can generate a novel caste by modifying a specific preexisting larval population, providing a molecular genetic explanation for how novel phenotypes can arise, more broadly, through modification of ancestral developmental plasticity.

articles_hidden.title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis CpsA interferes with the TBK1-p62 axis to inhibit xenophagy
articles_hidden.authors: Jully J. Sadadiwala, Sharvath Kathi, Ekansh Mittal, Keysha Patel, Thomas J. Brett, Jennifer A. Philips
articles_hidden.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) survives in macrophages by interfering with host lysosomal trafficking. Previously, we demonstrated that the Mtb protein, CpsA, is critical for bacterial survival in macrophages and infection in mice and that it can inhibit a noncanonical autophagy pathway. We also found that CpsA can interact with NDP52 and TAX1BP1, selective autophagy receptors that recognize cytosolic bacteria and target them for degradation, raising the possibility that CpsA also disrupts canonical autophagy. Here, we show that CpsA binds NDP52 and TAX1BP1 in their SKICH domains, which normally recruit the autophagy initiation machinery and TBK1. We demonstrate that CpsA prevents phagosomal recruitment of FIP200, a component of the autophagy initiation machinery, and blocks TBK1-dependent phosphorylation of p62, leading to impaired xenophagy. Our findings provide mechanistic insight into how Mtb subverts host defenses, revealing that in addition to blocking noncanonical autophagy, CpsA inhibits the TBK1-p62 axis to block xenophagy.

articles_hidden.title: Intestinal BMP SMADs impart the mid-villus pattern through a transcription factor cascade mechanism
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Logerfo, Jahangir Iqbal, Rachel Ofer, Sneha Kandalgaonkar, Rahma Rizly, Ping He, Merilyn Anusha Gnanapragasam, Marielle Rodney, Kiranmayi Vemuri, Lei Chen, Martin Matzuk, Michael P. Verzi
articles_hidden.abstract: Differentiated cells of the intestinal villus are not a monolith of equivalent cell types, but an exquisitely patterned continuum of transdifferentiated cells with evolving functions. Villus patterning requires BMP signaling; however, the transcriptional regulators downstream of BMP are unclear. We find that SMAD1 and SMAD5 are necessary for middle villus pattern. Spatial transcriptomics reveal a homeotic-like shift in the villus pattern of SMAD1/SMAD5 mutants, with the villus bottom and tip domains expanding at the expense of the middle. Disruption of mid-villus patterning corresponds to decreases in lipid uptake and runted pups in SMAD1/5 mutants. Unexpectedly, SMAD1/5 is not required for regulation of villus tip identity, which is dependent on SMAD4. Epigenomics approaches reveal a mechanism in which SMAD1/5 directly activate some mid-villus genes and control others via a transcription factor hierarchy, including TBX3. An intestine-specific TBX3 mutant phenocopied the SMAD1/5 mutant. These findings contribute mechanistic details to intestinal villus patterning.

articles_hidden.title: Small and large earthquakes driven by inelastic deformation in weak fault zones
articles_hidden.authors: Peng Zhai, Yihe Huang, Jean-Paul Ampuero
articles_hidden.abstract: Earthquakes manifest across a wide range of magnitudes, corresponding to a diversity of rupture sizes and amounts of slip. Classical earthquake models consider rupture processes solely on the fault plane, but the surrounding fault zone rocks can host inelastic deformation. Here, we show, via a dynamic seismic cycle model incorporating spontaneous fault zone evolution through damage and healing, that both small and large earthquakes on a single fault emerge naturally from the interplay of fault slip and fault zone inelastic deformation. Our simulations reproduce key observations: frequency-magnitude distribution consistent with the Gutenberg-Richter law, magnitude-invariant static stress drop, and the dual-regime scaling of fracture energy density with earthquake magnitude. The results underscore the coevolution of earthquakes and fault zone damage as a fundamental mechanism governing earthquake behavior in nature. Fault zone deformation causing multiscale seismicity indicates that continuous monitoring of fault zone material properties may reveal fault stress states and earthquake potential.

articles_hidden.title: Sequential anion chemistry enables dynamic interphase regulation in high-voltage LiCoO 2
articles_hidden.authors: Lu Chen, Kai Cui, Guoqiang He, Yanxin Jiang, Chunlei Song, Nanshan Chen, Zhiqiang Yang, Junjie Chen, Chun Zeng, Tianshuai Wang, Wenjia Li, Zhouguang Lu, Tianshou Zhao, Yiju Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Lithium-ion batteries using LiCoO 2 cathodes have powered portable electronics for decades, yet their operation above 4.5 volts remains severely constrained by the unstable evolution of the cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI). Under high-voltage conditions, lattice oxygen release and continuous electrolyte oxidation progressively degrade interfacial integrity. Here, we report a diluent-mediated local solvation regulation strategy to decrease dissociative solvent molecules and induce dual anion selective redistribution around Li + , forming a sequential solvation motif that drives sequential anion interfacial chemistry. DFOB − preferentially decomposes to establish a robust initial CEI framework, while BF 4 − continuously drives interfacial reactions to dynamically repair CEI defects and quench reactive oxygen species generated from lattice oxygen release. This dynamic regulation mechanism effectively stabilizes LiCoO 2 under aggressive high-voltage cycling. Consequently, the LiCoO 2 cathode delivers stable performance for 500 cycles at 4.5 volts with 73.5% capacity retention even in a low-concentration ether-based electrolyte. Furthermore, graphite||LiCoO 2 pouch cell achieves an energy density of 265.8 watt-hours per kilogram and exhibits favorable low-temperature resilience, retaining 99.1% capacity after 700 cycles at −20°C. These findings provide critical mechanistic insights into how solvation structure–driven anion chemistry can govern interfacial stability and unlock high-voltage, extreme-condition lithium-ion batteries.

articles_hidden.title: DFT-assisted natural abundance 13 C zero-field NMR via optical magnetometry
articles_hidden.authors: Blake Andrews, Xiao Liu, Raphael Zumbrunn, Calvin Lee, Sahand Adibnia, Emanuel Druga, Martin Head-Gordon, Ashok Ajoy
articles_hidden.abstract: Zero-field (ZF) nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy probes nuclear J-couplings without homogeneous magnetic fields, enabling inexpensive and geometrically flexible detection, including through metal. However, its broader use for chemical analysis has been limited by sensitivity and the difficulty of predicting the dense ZF multiplets. Here we demonstrate natural-abundance (1.1%) carbon-13 ( 13 C) ZF spectroscopy on off-the-shelf liquids using a compact commercial rubidium-87 magnetometer without hyperpolarization or special preparation. Instrumental advances yield improved sensitivity, ≤250-millihertz linewidths, and >week-long stability, enabling isotopomer-resolved fingerprint spectra across a 13-molecule library, including rare (0.0121%) doubly 13 C-labeled species. In parallel, we demonstrate vibrationally corrected density functional theory (DFT) prediction of ZF spectra with good qualitative agreement. Comparing experiment with these calculations renders residual deviations as chemically informative, reporting on hydrogen bonding and ion pairing at high ionic strength. These results contribute toward DFT-assisted ZF NMR as a general platform for field constraint–free molecular identification and for extracting transient solution-state structure from responsive J-coupling observables.

articles_hidden.title: Machine-learning-driven identification of cooperative descriptors for polysulfide conversion on spinel oxides
articles_hidden.authors: Wen Xie, Wen Cui, Kai Tang, Shibo Xi, Zihan Shen, Longcheng Zhang, Dongshuang Wu, Zhichuan J. Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: Spinel oxides have emerged as promising catalysts for polysulfide conversion, yet a comprehensive design strategy that elucidates the underlying structure–property relationship across diverse spinel oxides remains elusive. The complex multistep conversion processes make single descriptors insufficient to capture the full catalytic behavior, whereas identifying cooperative descriptors introduces additional complexity that challenges manual analysis. Here, we employ a machine-learning–assisted approach to uncover universal cooperative descriptors and accelerate the discovery of high-performance spinel catalysts. We reveal that the intrinsic polysulfide conversion efficiency of spinel oxides is cooperatively governed by two structural features. Further screening of promising catalysts is conducted using the extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithm, achieving rapid and accurate prediction of these features on spinel oxides. The model identifies Fe 2 CoO 4 and Fe 2 NiO 4 as superior catalysts, which are experimentally validated to exhibit excellent performance. This work provides deep mechanistic insights and a powerful data-driven framework for the rational design of spinel catalysts, with potential extension to other applications.

articles_hidden.title: Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens ’ dispersal
articles_hidden.authors: Marco Vidal-Cordasco, Guillermo Rodríguez-Gómez, Ana B. Marín-Arroyo
articles_hidden.abstract: To what extent Neanderthal extinction was triggered by climate change or the arrival of Homo sapiens , and by which mechanisms, remains unresolved. Here, on the basis of climate-driven changes in habitat favorability for primary and secondary consumers and in net primary productivity, we estimate carrying capacity, herbivore biomass, and intraguild predation pressure during the time Neanderthals and H. sapiens lived in Europe. These spatially explicit estimates were incorporated into an agent-based model simulating human demographic dynamics under various scenarios. Results indicate that carrying capacity changes cannot explain Neanderthal extinction at a continental scale, though they are essential to understanding spatiotemporal distribution patterns of both human species. Conversely, the arrival of H. sapiens remarkably increased Neanderthal extinction likelihood. Because of the successive demographic expansions and contractions, group connectivity emerges as the key factor shaping population stability in both species. These findings support that Neanderthal disappearance and H. sapiens dispersals were interconnected demographic processes.

articles_hidden.title: Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6
articles_hidden.authors: Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu, Guochun Zhao
articles_hidden.abstract: South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin has recorded complex geological histories of the Moon. It is a critical region for solving lunar fundamental questions but remained unexplored until the Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6 missions of China. Their in situ measurements and the Chang’e-6 samples provided the first ground truth for the SPA evolution. On the basis of these constraints, we found that the SPA impact occurred ∼4.34 billion years ago, generating a thick melt sheet that differentiated to form moderately magnesium (Mg)–rich norites. They are exposed at the SPA central peaks and currently investigated by the Chang’e-4 mission in Von Kármán crater, transported by the Finsen impact to the site. Highly Mg-rich materials were found within SPA, likely products of Mg-suite magmatism, including those exposed at the Apollo western peak ring. They were initially excavated by the Apollo impact at ∼4.2 billion years ago and delivered to the Chang’e-6 site by the Chaffee S impact. A series of other events occurred in the SPA basin subsequently (e.g., the Orientale impact ∼3.87 billion years ago); all of them shaped the architecture of the Moon’s largest impact basin.

articles_hidden.title: Environment-adaptive molecular neural networks enabled by heterogeneous threshold DNA neuron
articles_hidden.authors: Xiewei Xiong, Wanhui Xu, Na Li, Sichen Xing, Ziyi Huang, Jiayi Chen, Li Li, Tong Zhu, Hao Pei
articles_hidden.abstract: Molecular neural networks enable autonomous information processing in biochemical environments, yet most existing DNA-based implementations operate with fixed connectivity after assembly, limiting their ability to adapt network topology to changing environments. Here, we report an environment-adaptive molecular neural network enabled by DNA neurons with sequence-programmed, heterogeneous activation thresholds. These neurons incorporate triplex-based proton-gated DNA switches with tunable pH-response windows, which regulate the accessibility of toehold and recognition domains to switch pre-encoded weighted connections between inactive and signal-propagating states, thereby reconfiguring network connectivity without changing molecular composition. We demonstrate this principle in a DNA neural network that processes 64-bit inputs, where environmental acidification activates dormant neurons and reconfigures the computational topology from a sparse convolutional neural network for coarse two-class categorization into a fully connected neural network for fine-grained discrimination among four distinct patterns. Our results establish DNA-based neural circuits capable of adapting their computational architecture to environmental cues, offering a framework for molecular information processing in fluctuating biochemical environments.

articles_hidden.title: Platelet glycoprotein Ib shapes the immune response during lung injury
articles_hidden.authors: David Köhler, Anna Biedritzky, Philipp Burkard, Chunguang Liang, Linyan Tang, Alice Bernard, Philipp Dignus, Tim Steiner, Tiago F. Granja, Claudia Eggstein, Chao Liu, Lina M. Serna-Higuita, Diana Dudziak, Thomas Dandekar, Valbona Mirakaj, Bernhard Nieswandt, Peter Rosenberger
articles_hidden.abstract: The acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a life-threatening, inflammatory disease state of the lung. Self-propagating inflammation within the alveolar space and excessive infiltration of neutrophils into the pulmonary airspace are the main mechanisms underlying the dysfunction. A role of platelets in the pathogenesis of ARDS is suggested, but the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. We hypothesized that platelet glycoprotein (GP)Ib is an important contributor of platelet activation in this context. To highlight the contribution of the GPIb to the acute phase of experimental ALI in mice, we exposed mice genetically lacking functional GPIb ( GPIb-IL-4tg ) and wild-type (WT) mice injected with a function blocking anti-GPIb antibody to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) inhalation. GPIb-IL-4tg mice as well as anti-GPIb–treated mice displayed reduced neutrophil infiltration of the alveolar space in response to LPS. GPIb-IL-4tg mice as well as anti-GPIb–treated WT mice showed reduced interactions of platelets with neutrophils in comparison to controls, resulting in reduced platelet-neutrophil complexes and mitigated formation of neutrophil extracellular traps. Since these mechanisms are important for defense against external invasion of pathogens, we exposed GPIb-IL-4tg mice to Klebsiella pneumoniae and found reduced survival with increased bacterial load in these animals. Last, translational evaluation of biosamples of patients with ARDS showed that patients with low plasma levels of the shed GPIbα ectodomain (glycocalicin) exhibited higher mortality and worsened overall outcome. Together, our study shows that GPIb is a central mediator of neutrophil migration into the alveolar space and the defense mechanisms against the external invasion of pathogens.

articles_hidden.title: SMAD4 loss drives cancer chromosomal instability through transcription-replication conflict–associated replication stress
articles_hidden.authors: Atmika Paul, Gargee Joshi, Philipp Jungk, Simranjeet Kaur, Shengyu Yao, Ioannis Tsirkas, Nicolas Böhly, Maren Sitte, Gabriela Salinas, Stephan Hamperl, Maik Kschischo, Holger Bastians
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancer chromosomal instability (CIN) drives tumor evolution through generating structural and numerical chromosome aberrations. However, its molecular determinants remain poorly characterized. Here, we uncover a yet unrecognized role for the tumor suppressor SMAD4 as a key regulator of chromosomal stability. Mechanistically, loss of SMAD4 causes replication stress by promoting transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs) and induces subsequent mitotic errors, leading to the concomitant emergence of structural and numerical CIN. While the tumor suppressor function of SMAD4 has been predominantly attributed to transforming growth factor–β signaling, we find that its role in genome maintenance operates via bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling and its transcriptional target gene ID3 . Consequently, inhibition of BMP signaling mimics the loss of SMAD4 , while reexpression of SMAD4 or ID3 in SMAD4 -deficient colorectal or pancreatic cancer cells suppresses TRCs, replication stress, and mitotic errors. Our findings reveal a TRC- and replication stress–driven mechanism by which loss of BMP-SMAD4 signaling causes cancer CIN.

articles_hidden.title: Self-assembly of bacterial volumetric patterns directed by a synthetic reaction-diffusion circuit
articles_hidden.authors: Fuqing Wu, Changhan He, Samat Bayakhmetov, Duane Harris, Xin Fang, Javier Baez, Steven Ohnmacht, Qi Zhang, Xingwen Chen, Kyle R. Allison, Yang Kuang, Xiao Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Reaction-diffusion (RD) has long been proposed as a mechanism underlying biological pattern formation. However, quantitative frameworks linking circuit design to spatial organization remain limited. Here, we engineered a synthetic gene circuit, MINPAC, that couples gene expression regulation (reaction) with bacterial colony expansion and quorum sensing (diffusion) to guide bacterial cells to self-organize into periodic volumetric patterns across multiple scales, from single cells to three-dimensional colonies. The patterns exhibit robustness against environmental variations and size-dependent complexity. Mathematical modeling supports a clock-and-wavefront mechanism, where oscillatory gene expression interacts with outward expanding diffusions to generate these periodic spatial structures. Topological analysis reveals that specific network architecture is essential for pattern formation. Guided by model predictions, we further show that pattern complexity can be systematically tuned by gene dosage, with lower expression levels favoring multiple rings through faster dynamics. This work establishes a framework uniting circuit engineering and mathematical analysis for programming multicellular self-organization through RD mechanisms, with potential applications in regenerative medicine and biomaterials.

articles_hidden.title: Enzymatic degradation of a polyester-based thermoset composite resin by an engineered cutinase from Fusarium solani
articles_hidden.authors: Mikel Dolz, Matheo Berthet, Beatrice Mongili, Nuria Velasco, Alain Garillot, Julio Vidal-Navarro, Javier Viña-Gonzalez, Miguel Alcalde
articles_hidden.abstract: Thermoset composites have become indispensable high-performance materials across key industrial sectors. However, existing recycling methods have yet to deliver sustainable end-of-life solutions for these materials. Here, we report the engineering of a highly active and stable biocatalyst capable of depolymerizing polyester-based thermoset composites. First, a second-generation polyester resin was designed to enhance susceptibility to enzymatic attack. Cutinase from Fusarium solani was selected and subsequently engineered through a combination of directed evolution and computational design using two soluble surrogate motifs representative of the redesigned resin structure. The resulting variant, which incorporated 19 mutations, exhibited a 22-fold increase in activity and an 11°C improvement in melting temperature while achieving recombinant production titers at the gram-per-liter scale in yeast cultivated in fed-batch bioreactor. This engineered enzyme depolymerized the polyester resin with a total release of 6 mM (∼1.08 grams per liter) monomethyl phthalate. Together, to our knowledge, these findings constitute the first documented example of enzymatic degradation of a complex polyester resin from thermoset composite materials.

articles_hidden.title: Roseburia intestinalis counteracts TBEP-exacerbated atherosclerosis
articles_hidden.authors: Liangju Liu, Tiantian Gan, Liu Yang, Zhiwei Wang, Xiaowang Lv, Xiaoyan Wang, Ka Zhang, Hao Kan, Mengru Gao, Lilong Pan, Aiqin Mao, Tingting Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Interactions between serum metabolites and vascular endothelial cells directly influence atherosclerotic lesions. It is essential to identify and understand the effects of the complex profile of serum metabolites on vascular pathology. In this study, we found that coronary lesion severity positively correlated with serum levels of the organophosphate ester tris (2-butoxyethyl) phosphate (TBEP), while TBEP levels inversely correlated with gut Roseburia intestinalis abundance. Western diet supplemented with TBEP substantially exacerbated atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein E −/− ( ApoE −/− ) mice. We found that TBEP enhanced AMP-activated protein kinase α (AMPKα) phosphorylation, reduced nuclear translocation of active sterol regulatory element–binding protein 1c (SREBP1c) fragments, suppressed Patatin-like phospholipase domain–containing protein 3 (PNPLA3) protein expression in endothelial cells, and increased lipid deposition. Oral R. intestinalis supplementation reduced fecal and serum TBEP levels and attenuated TBEP-driven atherosclerotic lesions. We highlight that TBEP aggravates endothelial lipid accumulation and atherosclerosis, suggesting that targeting gut microbiota may serve as a promising strategy against TBEP-exacerbated atherosclerosis.

articles_hidden.title: Solubility-driven morphological decoupling enables elastic electron-deficient semiconducting polymers for fully stretchable electronics
articles_hidden.authors: Hayeong Park, Qian Liu, Wenhao Li, Minji Chung, Gunmo Koo, Chien-Chung Shih, Christopher R. McNeill, Dongsheng Yan, Yang Wang, Shanshan Zhou, Mandar M. Shirolkar, Ruicheng Li, Aung Ko Ko Kyaw, Yunqi Liu, Prashant Sonar, Joon Hak Oh
articles_hidden.abstract: The development of fully stretchable electronics is limited by the scarcity of electron-deficient polymers that combine high electron mobility with mechanical elasticity. Here, we report a solubility-driven morphological decoupling strategy that mitigates this trade-off by incorporating ∼10% planar, insoluble PyF units into a semicrystalline PySe backbone. This approach yields a hierarchical morphology characterized by suppressed long-range crystallinity alongside robust local aggregation. Driven by strong fluorine (F)-sulfur (S) interactions, highly ordered face-on domains function as robust physical anchors, providing the polymer network with exceptional elasticity to reversibly dissipate stress and preserve charge percolation pathways. Consequently, the resulting terpolymer largely relieves the long-standing trade-off between charge transport and mechanical stretchability, delivering a near-unity initial electron mobility (∼1.0 square centimeter per volt per second) and retaining 0.5 square centimeters per volt per second even under 100% applied strain, representing the highest performance reported to date. To demonstrate the practical utility of this system, we fabricated stretchable ambipolar inverters and phototransistors that maintain high performance under severe deformation. Notably, the phototransistors sustain an exceptional responsivity of 15.8 amperes per watt and an external quantum efficiency exceeding 2900% at 100% strain. These results establish a powerful blueprint for intrinsically elastic semiconductors, enabling the realization of high-performance, fully deformable optoelectronic systems.

articles_hidden.title: Evolution of MEIS transcription factor activity during metazoan neural development—born to be wild
articles_hidden.authors: Pavel Fedarenchik, Hanna Polevoy, Yael Volovik, Emil Aamar, Mohammed Mahroum, Gilad Barshad, Adi Salzberg, Dale Frank
articles_hidden.abstract: Meis TALE-class proteins pattern vertebrate neural tissue, inducing hindbrain and neural crest in Xenopus laevis embryos. Meis orthologs have two conserved regions: (i) Meis-specific domain and (ii) Meis-specific TALE homeodomain. Meis homeodomain proteins are present in “ancient” metazoans-eucaryotes like cnidarians, placozoans, and protozoans. We asked: When during metazoan evolution did Meis proteins acquire functionality to induce neural pattern? Using structure-function analysis in Xenopus , we show that the Meis-specific and Meis homeodomains suffice to induce the spinal cord but not the hindbrain. Meis proteins share a functionally conserved carboxyl-terminal transcription activation domain inducing the hindbrain. Ancient Meis proteins from Trichoplax and chlorophyte algae have a conserved Meis homeodomain, but lack the Meis-specific domain. Unexpectedly, these ancestral proteins robustly induce hindbrain and neural crest in Xenopus , unlike metazoan proteins requiring the Meis-specific domain. Thus, in early eukaryotes, Meis prototypes were “born to be wild,” having the intrinsic capacity to induce vertebrate structures like hindbrain and neural crest, despite predating them.

articles_hidden.title: SeqA-mediated sister loci cohesion regulates the efficiency and fidelity of DNA double-strand break repair across the E. coli genome
articles_hidden.authors: Deepak K. Singh, Amir Faraz, Nuha A. Khan, Jebin Babu, T. Sabari Sankar, David Bates, Mohan C. Joshi
articles_hidden.abstract: In Escherichia coli , SeqA-mediated cohesion at snap loci on the right replichore persists longer, but its role in DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair remains untested. Here, we show that site-specific DSBs at snap loci confer higher cell survival than nonsnap loci. With perturbations affecting sister cohesion [Δ seqA , topoisomerase IV overexpression (T4-OE)], this survival advantage was progressively reduced, with the combined Δ seqA T4-OE strain retaining only a transient advantage. The increased survival correlates with faster repair, reflected by rapid restoration of locus copy number and shorter-lived, thinner RecA–green fluorescent protein filaments. Consistent with more accurate repair, snap loci exhibited lower mutation accumulation under normal and antibiotic stress conditions. Comparative genome analysis of E. coli strains revealed higher GATC motif counts and higher sequence conservation. Together, these findings suggest that the chromosomal organization associated with prolonged sister cohesion at snap loci promotes efficient homologous recombination–mediated DSB repair and contributes to genome conservation.

articles_hidden.title: TLR5 drives metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis through lipid- and flagellin-induced hepatocyte injury signaling
articles_hidden.authors: Wenhao Li, Niannian Wang, Dania El Abyad, Seray Anak, Raju Kumar, Iris Ginés, Upkar Gill, Gillian Hood, James Brindley, Charles Mein, James Boot, Una Rose Wilcox, Neil Dufton, Robert Goldin, Tania Roskams, John Loy, Kalpana Devalia, Humza Malik, Adam Goralcyzk, Maria Jimenez-Ramos, Timothy J. Kendall, Jonathan A. Fallowfield, Maria Ines Castanho Martins, Krista Rombouts, Michele Vacca, Olivier Govaere, William Alazawi
articles_hidden.abstract: Liver fibrosis is a strong predictor of clinical outcomes in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Fibrosis is a consequence of persistent liver cell injury and inflammation in which Toll-like receptors (TLRs) play a key initiating role. Here, we test the hypothesis that TLR5 is involved in the development of MASH and fibrosis using a combination of clinical data from multiple independent patient cohorts, single-cell liver transcriptomics, and human in vitro and ex vivo models. Hepatic TLR5 expression, but not TLR2 or TLR4, is associated with liver fibrosis and mortality. Plasma levels of TLR5’s cognate ligand flagellin are increased in MASH with advanced fibrosis and fall with liver disease improvement. Mechanistically, we identify two parallel TLR5-mediated routes to hepatocyte injury: one elicited by flagellin and the other indirectly by lipid injury. Furthermore, hepatocyte TLR5 inhibition abrogates paracrine activation of hepatic stellate cells to suppress collagen production. This is also seen ex vivo in patient-derived precision-cut liver slices where TLR5 inhibition significantly reduces lipid-induced collagen deposition. These findings reveal a new role for TLR5 signaling, specifically in the development of advanced MASH fibrosis and may offer a novel disease-specific therapeutic approach.

articles_hidden.title: An all-magnonic neuron with tunable fading memory
articles_hidden.authors: David Breitbach, Moritz Bechberger, Hanadi Mortada, Björn Heinz, Roman Verba, Qi Wang, Carsten Dubs, Mario Carpentieri, Giovanni Finocchio, Davi Rodrigues, Alexandre Abbass Hamadeh, Philipp Pirro
articles_hidden.abstract: Magnonics offers nanometer-scale wave propagation and strong nonlinearities, making it attractive for neuromorphic applications such as artificial neurons. Yet, magnonic elements with interconnections solely within the magnonic system remain challenging, preventing the realization of interconnected magnonic neurons to date. Here, we experimentally demonstrate an all-magnonic neuron that reacts to magnon inputs with thresholded, amplified magnon firing and subsequent self-reset, enabling all-magnonic operation and cascading. Our approach is based on micro-antenna excitation on an ultralow damping garnet with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, where we exploit the positive magnon frequency shift to realize nonlinear activation. Using Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy, we uncover a transient neuron response with tunable fading memory: A 25% change in pump power results in a three-order-of-magnitude tuning in memory time, which we harness, demonstrating temporal integration of up to 50 magnon pulses. Last, we realize neuron triggering in a cascade of three neurons, highlighting its potential for connected magnonic circuits.

articles_hidden.title: Targeting METTL3 protects against acetaminophen-induced liver injury through HAPTOGLOBIN/CD163 macrophage axis
articles_hidden.authors: Huaxin Chen, Silin Tu, Bo Cui, Zhancheng Zeng, Xuanyong Chen, Shuai Dong, Yanli Li, Shanshan Yu, Xiao Liu, Ruiqi Xiao, Jing Guo, Xiaoqi Liang, Lijie Pan, Jiajie Chu, Yiju Huang, Chang Liu, Guo Lv, Yiwang Zhang, Wenjie Chen, Qi Zhang, Yan Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is the most common cause of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), with limited treatment options. N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) is the most abundant internal epitranscriptomic modification in eukaryotic RNAs and is involved in various physiological and pathological processes, serving as a potential therapeutic target for many diseases. However, little is known about the role of m 6 A in DILI. Here, we found that intrahepatic expression of Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), the core catalytic subunit of RNA m 6 A methyltransferase complex, was elevated in patients with DILI and mouse DILI models. Hepatocyte-specific knockout of METTL3, achieved via either Alb-Cre ERT2 –driven recombination or adeno-associated virus (AAV)–mediated delivery of Cre, significantly protected from APAP-induced hepatotoxicity in both male and female mice. Mechanistically, hepatic METTL3 deficiency reduced m 6 A deposition on acute-phase protein haptoglobin ( Hp ) transcripts and promoted Hp transcription and translation in hepatocytes. Increased HP secreted by hepatocytes bound to its receptor CD163, expressed explicitly on macrophages, and induced highly phagocytic and anti-inflammatory polarization of macrophages, finally reducing APAP-induced hepatic injury. Moreover, two different METTL3 inhibitors, JNJ64619178 and STM2457, effectively alleviated APAP-induced liver injury. Our study thus demonstrated that hepatic inhibition of METTL3 protected against APAP-induced liver injury by promoting the cross-talk between hepatocytes and macrophages through HP/CD163, underscoring the potential of targeting METTL3 as a promising therapy for APAP overdose.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond metabolites: A wearable biointerface integrating antibody and aptamer probes for the real-time tracking of proteins in vivo
articles_hidden.authors: Hanjia Zheng, Fatima Shafique, Alexander S. Qian, Mayank Garg, Florian Gessler, Jonathan L’Heureux Hache, Quan M. Quach, Bernardo L. Trigatti, Mahla Poudineh, Leyla Soleymani
articles_hidden.abstract: Continuous monitoring of protein biomarkers could transform the management of acute and chronic diseases. Despite tremendous potential, wearable health monitors have remained largely limited to metabolites and small molecules. A key challenge is the limited availability of biointerfaces that reversibly track low-abundance proteins in vivo without user intervention. Here, we present the Differential Aptalyzer, a minimally invasive hydrogel microneedle platform for continuous monitoring of proteins in skin interstitial fluid. The platform combines high-affinity antibodies for selective target capture with aptamers for reversible electrochemical signal transduction. When integrated into a differential electrochemical chip and pulse-assisted sensor regeneration, this approach enables continuous monitoring of proteins in a wearable format. Using cardiac troponin I (cTnI) as a clinically relevant model analyte, Differential Aptalyzer offers a broad dynamic range (0.003 to 0.640 nanograms per milliliter) and strong specificity against interfering proteins. This platform reliably tracks both rising and falling exogenous cTnI levels injected into healthy mice, as well as endogenously elevated cTnI in a double-knockout mouse model of coronary artery disease, demonstrating its capability in continuous protein monitoring and identifying coronary artery disease cohorts.

articles_hidden.title: Posttranscriptional regulation by TIA1 and TIAL1 controls the transcriptional program enforcing T cell quiescence
articles_hidden.authors: Ines C. Osma-Garcia, Trang-My M. Nguyen, Orlane Maloudi, Mailys Mouysset, Dunja Capitan-Sobrino, Yann Aubert, Manuel D. Diaz-Muñoz
articles_hidden.abstract: Immune protection against infections relies on long-term maintenance of a highly diversified naïve T cell repertoire. Transcription factors cooperate to enforce T cell metabolic quiescence and maintenance. However, less is known about the posttranscriptional networks that preserve naïve T cells. Here, we describe the RNA binding proteins T cell antigen 1 (TIA1) and TIA-like 1 (TIAL1) as key promoters of CD4 and CD8 T cell quiescence. T cells deficient in TIA1 and TIAL1 undergo premature T cell activation, exhaustion, and death in the absence of cognate antigens. Mechanistically, TIA1 and TIAL1 promote the messenger RNA translation of quiescence-associated transcription factors such as forkhead box P1, lymphoid enhancer factor 1, and T cell factor 1 to restrain homeostatic T cell proliferation and activation. In summary, our study highlights a previously unrecognized dependency on posttranscriptional gene regulation by TIA1 and TIAL1 for implementing the quiescent transcriptional programs for long survival of T cells.

articles_hidden.title: Membrane-confined self-assembly enables localized bioorthogonal prodrug activation and selective cancer therapy
articles_hidden.authors: Wenjie Wang, Jiaxin Guo, Hong Han, Dan Yuan, Junfeng Shi
articles_hidden.abstract: Bioorthogonal prodrug activation offers a promising approach for site-specific drug release, significantly reducing the systemic toxicity associated with conventional chemotherapy. However, challenges remain in precisely controlling prodrug activation at the target site while maintaining optimal selectivity, reactivity, and potency. Here, we report a dual-targeting peptide, TzFFY p HH, that integrates on-membrane enzyme-instructed self-assembly (EISA) with bioorthogonal chemistry to enable selective chemotherapy. Exploiting the overexpression of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) on cancer cells, TzFFY p HH selectively anchors and self-assembles on the cancer cell membrane, enriching tetrazine (Tz) handles that act as bioorthogonal reactors to activate a trans -cyclooctene (TCO)-caged prodrug (TCO-Dox) for precise drug release. Upon topical administration, TzFFY p HH forms a hydrogel at subcutaneous tumor sites, enabling in situ prodrug activation for effective tumor inhibition. Notably, this localized chemotherapy elicits a potent antitumor immune response, which, when combined with anti-programmed death-1 antibody (αPD-1), synergistically potentiates therapeutic outcomes. By coupling supramolecular self-assembly with bioorthogonal reactivity on the cell membrane, this work establishes a chemically programmable platform for spatiotemporally controlled prodrug activation and provides a general strategy for integrating localized chemotherapy with immunotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Yasumi Otani, Emily Goodall, Vignesh Srinivasan, Neil J. Ball, Samuel F. H. Barnett, Youlim Hwang, Dominic P. Byrne, Tobias Zech, Juha Saarikangas, Benjamin T. Goult
articles_hidden.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine/threonine kinase essential for brain development and function. Mutations in CDKL5 cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy associated with impaired synapse formation and function. However, how CDKL5 mutations disrupt synaptic function remains unclear. Here, we show that the major neuronal isoform of CDKL5 contains a C-terminal PDZ domain–binding motif that mediates direct binding to PSD-95 and SHANK PDZ domains and recruits CDKL5 to the postsynaptic density. Disrupting this motif mislocalized CDKL5, reduced dendritic spine density, and impaired spine maturation. We also show that the CDKL5 kinase domain binds the R8 rod domain of the mechanosensitive scaffold talin. Mutation of the talin-binding interface or reduced cellular contractility altered CDKL5 positioning relative to focal adhesions. These findings define how CDKL5 is targeted to synapses, suggest that talin mechanoswitching may position CDKL5 kinase activity, and highlight the importance of C-terminal anchoring for interpreting pathogenic truncations.

articles_hidden.title: Bionic skin with hair follicle regeneration capability from acoustic fluids-mediated 3D printing
articles_hidden.authors: Xinyue Cao, Ruisi He, Zhuhao Wu, Yuanjin Zhao
articles_hidden.abstract: Tissue engineering holds substantial potential for constructing normal skin with appendages such as hair follicles, directly restoring skin’s complete physiological functions. The current challenge lies in recreating biomimetic hair follicle organs with high-level cell density and architecture. Here, we developed an acoustofluidic-assisted 3D bioprinting platform to fabricate bionic skins with efficient hair follicle regeneration capability. Pre-formed hair follicle germs, derived from co-cultured epidermal and dermal mesenchymal stem cells, were encapsulated within a hydrogel bioink. Controlled acoustic fields generated flow vortices that directed cell migration and promoted organized cellular assembly from initially disordered states. Guided cell aggregates were then patterned through bioprinting to construct a grid-structured bionic skin. This architecture provided stable 3D support while maintaining high porosity, enabling efficient gas exchange. The printed bionic skin exhibited well-organized spatial cell distribution, high cellular viability, and promising differentiation potential. Further in vivo experiments demonstrated the efficiency of the bionic skin in accelerating mature hair regeneration, showing promise for clinical alopecia treatment.

articles_hidden.title: Phonon-assisted endothermic triplet sensitization enables record NIR-II-to-visible-light photon upconversion
articles_hidden.authors: Kin Ting Chang, Pui Ying Wong, Shaokuan Gong, Aleksandr A. Sergeev, Kai Kin Li, Kam Sing Wong, Xihan Chen, Haipeng Lu
articles_hidden.abstract: Near-infrared-to-visible triplet−triplet annihilation photon upconversion (TTA-UC) enables harvesting low-energy photons; however, extending nanocrystal-sensitized TTA-UC into the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) remains challenging because triplet sensitization is thermodynamically disfavored under sub-triplet excitation. Here, we demonstrate that lead-free AgBiS 2 nanocrystals facilitate phonon-assisted endothermic triplet sensitization, enabling efficient NIR-II-to-visible upconversion. Under the sub-bandgap single-photon excitation, AgBiS 2 nanocrystals exhibit anti-Stokes photoluminescence, suggesting strong exciton−phonon coupling mediated by surface states. When coupled with 5-tetracene carboxylic acid transmitters and rubrene annihilators, AgBiS 2 achieves 980 nm-to-visible upconversion with a record quantum yield of 6.22% (normalized to 100%) and an anti-Stokes shift of 0.95 eV. Time-resolved photoluminescence and ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy support a surface-state-mediated uphill energy-transfer pathway coupled to low-frequency vibrational modes. Our work establishes phonon-assisted triplet sensitization as a strategy to overcome the NIR-II red wall for lead-free photon upconversion.

articles_hidden.title: Anisotropic field suppression of charge order reveals orbital-selective Kondo hybridization in UTe 2
articles_hidden.authors: Nileema Sharma, Fangjun Cheng, Hyeok-Jun Yang, Matthew Toole, James McKenzie, Mitchell M. Bordelon, Sean M. Thomas, Priscila F. S. Rosa, Yi-Ting Hsu, Xiaolong Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: UTe 2 is a rare correlated quantum material where unconventional density-wave orders, Kondo physics, spin-triplet pairing, and reentrant superconductivity coexist. Because superconductivity emerges from a strongly correlated normal state, identifying and controlling intertwined normal-state orders are essential for understanding the electronic landscape where superconductivity arises. Here, using scanning tunneling microscopy in a vector magnetic field, we uncover a staggered charge density wave (CDW) in high-quality UTe 2 crystals. This CDW exhibits a strong directional field response: It is completely quenched by a modest 1.7-tesla magnetic field along the quasi–one-dimensional uranium-chain direction while remaining robust against fields along other crystallographic axes. This anisotropy suggests an orbital-driven field-tuned quantum phase transition. Unexpectedly, the same field orientation concurrently suppresses the 5f Kondo resonance. Modeling indicates a switch in the dominant hybridization channel from Te 5 p- U 5 f to U 6 d- U 5 f coupling, suggesting an intimate interplay between CDW and the Kondo effect.

articles_hidden.title: LONP-1 deficiency causes dysregulated protein synthesis within mitochondria that is suppressed by mitoribosomal mutations
articles_hidden.authors: Levi D. Ali, Avijit Mallick, Yunguang Du, Rui Li, Lihua J. Zhu, Kuang Shen, Cole M. Haynes
articles_hidden.abstract: Mitochondrial homeostasis is maintained by molecular chaperones and proteases located within the organelle. The mitochondrial matrix-localized protease LONP-1 degrades oxidatively damaged or misfolded proteins. Importantly, LONP-1 also regulates mitochondrial DNA replication. Here, we show that mutations in C. elegans that impair LONP-1 function cause dysregulation of mitochondrial DNA replication, mitochondrial RNA transcription and protein synthesis within the mitochondrial matrix. LONP-1 deficient worms had reduced levels of oxidative phosphorylation proteins despite increased mtDNA-encoded protein synthesis. Via a forward genetic screen, we identified three mutations that restored mitochondrial function and the rate of development in lonp-1 mutants to levels comparable to those in wildtype worms. Interestingly, all three suppressor mutations were found in genes encoding mitochondrial ribosome proteins. A point mutation in the mitochondrial ribosome protein MRPS-38 restored oxidative phosphorylation in lonp-1 mutant worms. Combined, our results suggest that LONP-1 regulates mitochondrial translation and that suppressor mutations within mrps-38 or mrps-15 can enhance oxidative phosphorylation complex assembly when LONP-1 function is diminished.

articles_hidden.title: Denoised vibrometry reveals noncanonical filtering at the apex of the cochlea
articles_hidden.authors: George W. S. Burwood, Pierre Hakizimana, Karl Grosh, Wajiha Zaidi, Ruikang K. Wang, Alfred L. Nuttall, Anders Fridberger
articles_hidden.abstract: How do mammals distinguish sounds with different pitch? Prevailing theory states that each position along the cochlear spiral responds best to one single stimulus frequency, forming a frequency-to-place (tonotopic) map that is preserved throughout the auditory pathways. Whether this holds in the low-frequency cochlear apex, a region important for vocal communication but technically challenging to study, is unknown. Using a differential noise-canceling technique, we recorded sound-evoked motion near the lower limit of hearing. Apical locations often had two best frequencies, contradicting the assumption of one-to-one frequency-to-place mapping. Spatially distant regions responded similarly, and brief sounds evoked synchronized motion across large distances, revealing an unusual energy propagation mode. Morphology and mathematical analyses corroborate these findings, showing that tonotopy breaks down at the apex of the cochlea. These results have important implications for cochlear implants, which currently assume tonotopic organization throughout the cochlea.

articles_hidden.title: Interfacing ultrafast single-photon-level fields with an atomic ensemble
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Shinbrough, Tegan Loveridge, Benjamin D. Hunt, Sehyun Park, Kathleen Oolman, Thomas O. Reboli, J. Gary Eden, Virginia O. Lorenz
articles_hidden.abstract: Ultrafast photons—with pulse durations on the order of 100 femtoseconds—are typical of high-rate, high-purity, entangled photon-pair sources. Efficient, coherent mapping between these states and matter-based quantum systems is an important problem in quantum optics and could enable applications in quantum frequency conversion, bandwidth conversion, and local quantum information processing at gigahertz speeds. This coherent mapping is also the initial storage step in matter-based photonic quantum memory, which can enhance multiphoton rates and allow for synchronization in quantum repeaters. Here, we use a collisionally broadened neutral atomic barium ensemble to demonstrate a quantum-compatible light-matter interface with storage efficiency of 95.6 ± 0.3%, total internal efficiency of 31 ± 1%, and noise contributions of <10 −4 photons per pulse. Using the simultaneous efficiency, bandwidth, and noise performance of this interface, we perform a full amplitude and phase reconstruction via spectral interferometry of single-photon-level fields retrieved from the interface.

articles_hidden.title: Geophysics-informed hydrologic modeling reveals contrasting regolith and bedrock responses of headwater catchments to warming
articles_hidden.authors: Chen Xiong, Hang Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Predicting how warming reshapes headwater streamflow requires distinguishing shallow and deep subsurface contributions, which remain difficult to constrain in catchment-scale models. We use seismic P-wave velocity to partition the critical zone into regolith and fractured bedrock domains within a three-dimensional physically based model and develop a particle-based attribution method to quantify their streamflow contributions and source-water ages across realizations spanning diverse hydraulic configurations.
